The phrase was useful in old discussions because everyone knew which file to open first; it also created an inaccurate impression that the worker itself was some independent, nameable exit.

This page retains the name because old links and search terms were built around it. If a reader has only located the file in the repository, the old record still answers where to look first. What needs changing is the explanation: the file path is the starting point for tracing back, not a definition of the event's semantics.

`src/loaders/basis_transcoder.worker.js` is the only fixed code anchor in this record. It is an existing JavaScript module. When reading, first focus on three nearby locations: the module's own declaration, the dependencies it directly touches, and the relationship that leads here from the loader side. This keeps upper-layer wait conditions from being folded into the worker's name.

```text
BASIS loader-related clues
          |
          v
src/loaders/basis_transcoder.worker.js
          |
          +--> Local declaration
          |
          +--> Direct dependencies
          |
          `--> Return to the caller side to confirm the event meaning
```

The diagram above is not an execution sequence diagram. It is simply the browsing order used by the old record: first identify a locatable object in the file, then follow the existing dependency and call relationships outward. In the past, some people read this order as "the event must be emitted outward from the worker." That is an overinterpretation. The worker may sit in the middle of the path; based on the entry file alone, no conclusion can be drawn about the event's direction, name, or recipient.

The draft's original wording can be summarized as: when you encounter the follow-up action after BASIS is transcoded, go back to the worker first. This sentence was not removed because it reflects the tracing method that was effective at the time. The problem is not the "go back first" step; it is that this was later expanded into "the worker is the exit." A caller-side check is missing between the two.

The first is the file-level exit point: the code enters `basis_transcoder.worker.js` through the loader ancestry relationship and unfolds between the local declaration and direct dependencies. Direct dependencies are still worth reviewing from this file, but their role is limited to narrowing the reading scope. The old version treated "dependencies are visible" as "event meaning is visible"; this is the second easy-to-make leap.

Likewise, the loader ancestry relationship cannot substitute for the call relationship. Tracing back on the loader side shows where the BASIS clue enters this code; looking outward on the caller side is the only way to have a chance of confirming where continued processing occurs. The two paths meeting near the same file does not mean their semantics are resolved here.

The declaration in the file is the most suitable anchor, followed by its direct dependencies. If the requirement is to verify a particular event, reading should pause here once and switch to the caller side to find where that event is consumed. This saves time over repeatedly guessing at the event in the worker and avoids the misleading impression created by the old title.

R26.9 In the Interaction Convergence notes, `Nested loader completion and generator contract` and `Reversible media snapping` were placed in the same record. That is only because both are investigated starting from media objects; it doesn't mean they already share an implementation path.

The local entry point currently traceable is `src/inflators/media-loader.ts`. Near the file header, the following direct dependencies appear:

```ts
import { addComponent } from "bitecs";
import { HubsWorld } from "../app";
import { MediaLoader } from "../bit-components";
import { MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS } from "../bit-systems/media-loading";
```

This indicates that the file interacts with component writes, the Rooms world, `MediaLoader`, and loading flags. It isn't enough to establish who creates the media objects or where restoration occurs after an object's position is snapped.

Two ways of recording this were compared initially.

One approach combines media loading and snapping into a single "media complete" result: once the root object appears, all subsequent actions assume they can proceed. This is convenient, but it leaves no separate decision points for nested descendants, media associations, and position restoration.

The other keeps two tracks. The loading track covers only the preparation of the media object and its descendants; the snapping track covers only reversible position changes and whether anything beyond the position itself is affected. The two tracks can share the media object as a lookup entry point, but neither can speak for the other just because both occur in the same investigation.

Use the second approach initially. The decision is narrow in scope: this page does not equate snapping restoration with load completion, nor does it make the appearance of the root object the only loading completion condition.

The earlier investigation traced this path by searching for names such as `media_loader`, `media-loader`, media, and loader. Further work needs to follow the actual references. Open questions: where the completion condition for nested objects is; whether position restoration involves media references; whether the collision shape falls within the same action boundary as position restoration.

# Media Loading and Snapping Decision

This page was originally tucked into the media notes for R26.9 Interaction Convergence. `Nested loader completion and generator contract` and `Reversible media snapping` often came up in the same round of investigation, but their inclusion on the same page did not mean they already shared an implementation. The page was not split up later because the two records do start from the same media object and the same local file entry point; nor did the page merge them, because loading completion and position restoration have never been interchangeable descriptions of the same thing.

`src/inflators/media-loader.ts` has always been the reference point for tracing the loading side. The adjacent entries retained in the file header are as follows:

```ts
import { addComponent } from "bitecs";
import { HubsWorld } from "../app";
import { MediaLoader } from "../bit-components";
import { MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS } from "../bit-systems/media-loading";
```

These dependencies define the scope of objects covered by the page: component writes, the world context, `MediaLoader`, and loading flags. They do not specify the restored position for media snapping, nor do they separately identify all callers. This decision has therefore always treated the file path as a lookup point for the loading track, rather than using the filename to determine where the two requirements belong.

## 2023-05-24 | The Initial Split

The initial draft had a narrow goal: to keep media loading and reversible snapping from overwriting each other in the record. At the time, they were documented as two separate tracks.

The loading track asks when a media object can be considered finished preparing. Nested objects were brought up because looking only at the root object makes it difficult to describe the full relationship. The snapping track asks whether a change to an object's position can be undone, and exactly which other objects are involved in the undo. The two tracks can share the media object as a lookup starting point, but should not share a generic "complete".

The initial draft also retained a convenient but rough assumption at the time: once the root object is displayed, the loader can initially be treated as finished; if the object has been snapped, wait for subsequent position changes to put it back. This assumption served only to let the investigation at the time split into separate tracks first. It did not explain whether nested descendants had already been processed, or whether the on-screen position, media reference, and collision shape represented the same result.

The decision made that same day did not require a complete call graph. What could be recorded were two items to investigate: what the page should not call the state where the root object has appeared but nested objects are still unfinished; whether the media reference or collision shape still needs separate verification when the position returns to its original location. At the time, these were only questions, not counterexample-based conclusions that had already been reached.

## 2023-05-24 | The Old Proposal in the Margin

The initial draft had considered consolidating everything into a single "media complete" result. This proposal was very simple to express: the root object provides the result, and actions after loading and actions after snapping both depend only on it. If the record served only a single brief investigation, this wording would also be easy to explain.

But it requires a single result to convey several different meanings at once: whether descendants are ready, whether the root object has reached its completion point, whether the media association still exists, whether the position has been restored. If any one of these conditions is unmet, the record will only say "the media has not completed", without leaving an object to investigate further.

A different approach was chosen at the time: keep the loading and snapping tracks separate. This choice was not a claim that the source code consisted of two state machines that never interact, but a way to avoid prematurely creating an unsupported common endpoint on the page. The loading side continued investigating from `MediaLoader` and the loading markers; the snapping side continued tracing the actual references for `Reversible media snapping`. Media objects appearing in both only indicate that the two sides encounter adjacent issues.

This section of the old approach remains on the page not because it is still usable, but because it documents the source of several later misreadings. After multiple objects are collapsed into one result, "the root object is visible", "the media reference is usable", "the position has been rolled back" can all easily be written as the same sentence, making it impossible to know later which observation actually occurred.

## 2023-08-29 | Review addendum

The first actual review did not establish a complete end-to-end path, but instead narrowed what could be concluded from the file header.

`addComponent` indicates that this file participates in component writes; this does not mean that it creates all related components.`HubsWorld` indicates that the loading logic has a Rooms world context; this does not mean that the full execution order within the world tick is already known. The co-occurrence of `MediaLoader` and `MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS` is enough to trace a loading issue from this file back to adjacencies on the object and system sides; this does not mean that either name can replace the references for snapping rollback.

The review also revisited the old lookup method. Early investigation used names such as `media_loader`,`media-loader`, media, loader to find `src/inflators/media-loader.ts`. Name matching is still a suitable entry point, but implementation ownership cannot be inferred from it. The loading track has this file as a local entry point; this does not make the same file responsible for the snapping track.

This round downgraded "the root object is displayed" from a working conclusion back to an earlier observation. Having the root object on screen does not automatically answer what state the nested objects, loading markers, media associations or subsequent waits are in. If only the root object is observed, the record should state only that the root object has appeared, not casually expand that into a claim that the entire media tree has finished.

## 2023-08-29 | Retained but deprecated wording

> Once the root object is visible, the loader can be considered complete; undoing snapping only requires waiting for the position to refresh.

**Later overturned.** This passage was not deleted, because it illustrates the early loss of focus better than any retrospective write-up: treating appearance on screen as the end of loading, and treating some future position change as an inevitable recovery mechanism.

The first half of the statement left out the nesting relationship. The root object's on-screen state and its descendants' readiness are not synonymous. The second half left out the scope of the objects involved. A change in position does not mean the media reference necessarily changes, nor does it mean the collision shape has already been handled. The old sentence can no longer be used as a basis for judgment, but it leaves a practical reminder: any description that something has "come back" must first specify whether what came back was the position, the reference, or the shape.

A shorthand note that was not formally written up at the time was also retained alongside the review record: the loader only needs to be attached to the root node, and external callers can simply be left to wait for the child nodes to be ready themselves. This formulation is likewise no longer applicable. It did not identify the caller or explain the conditions under which the caller starts or stops waiting. Handing these gaps to an unconfirmed external entity merely moves the judgment away from the current page and does not resolve it.

## 2024-11-25 | Revising the Position After Field Feedback

Later field feedback meant the page was no longer organized around "whether the root node has appeared". The issue returned to the relationship between nested objects and the root object's completion. The earlier claim that the root object's visibility marked the end of the loader was therefore withdrawn; the earlier assumption that an unnamed caller would wait for the child nodes was withdrawn as well.

This change in position did not fill in all the execution details to create a new big picture. It only put the items that still needed verification back on the loading workstream: ancestry relationships, counts, the root object's completion record, media associations, content boundaries, and the actual conditions under which the waiting process ends. These had previously been obscured by the single short phrase "the media is ready", and now need to be retained separately.

The snapping workstream also stopped using "snapping only changes position" as its default judgment after this feedback. The existing records do not allow a position change to establish whether the media reference was read or restored, nor do they allow a position change to establish how the collision shape was handled. Snapping remains scoped to undoable position changes, but the page does not expand that scope into a confirmed rollback workflow.

The decision in this round of supplementary notes sets a clear stopping point: when the material only shows a position change, record only the position change; when the material shows a change in the media reference, list the media reference separately; shape information should likewise be recorded against the object it pertains to. When there is no shared reference linking them, the three cannot be described as a single recovery merely to make the sentence complete.

## 2024-11-25 | The Sequence Left in the Review Margins

The brief sequence left in the review record is: first confirm the completion point for the loader, then discuss the rollback point for snap; do not substitute "already displayed" for the completion point.

This does not demote snapping to a subsidiary step of loading. It emphasizes the prerequisite for making a judgment: when the loading completion point has not yet been clarified, appearance on screen cannot be used to infer whether snapping has already crossed a reliable boundary; conversely, merely observing a position change cannot be used to prove that loading has finished.

Next, this page placed a small constraint on terminology. When the discussion says "the media is back," the record must identify the specific object. Position is a change in space; a media reference is an association held by an object; a collision shape is shape information for a physical object. They may be observed around the same operation, but without evidence connecting them, they cannot be assumed to be three names for the same action.

One question has also been left in place on the same page: whether the snapping process will continue to process the same object after loading ends. This question has no answer, so it is not used to change the conclusion about loading, nor is it used to designate where responsibility for snapping lies.

## 2024-11-25 | Current Loading Requirements

The earlier old notes, discarded wording, file-header review, and on-the-spot changes in wording are all retained here for now, with the current position on loading set out below:

> Media loading is an ancestor-counted lifecycle: inflateMediaLoader attaches MediaLoader and MediaLoading, initializes MediaLoader.count and mediaRef, interns source/file identifiers, hides unfinished descendants, and completes the root once while recording MediaContentBounds.bounds; waitForMediaLoaded(world, eid) remains a frame-yielding generator until the loader is removed.

Ancestor counting here is not root-object visibility repackaged under another name. The loading lifecycle uses ancestor-based counting, and `inflateMediaLoader` attaches `MediaLoader` and `MediaLoading` and initializes `MediaLoader.count` and `mediaRef`. These objects provide a traceable location for loading state, which no longer relies solely on the root object on screen.

source/file identifiers are interned, so file identity should not be replaced by "it is already displayed on screen" either. Unfinished descendants are hidden, which is one of the reasons early visibility checks are unreliable: whether the root object is visible cannot, on its own, convey the completion semantics of the entire nested loading process.

Completion of the root object occurs only once, and `MediaContentBounds.bounds` is recorded at that point. Root-object completion, content-boundary recording, and handling of incomplete descendants should be treated as different points in the same loading lifecycle, rather than all being reduced to "the media is ready." `MediaContentBounds.bounds` also cannot be directly equated with a collision shape; the former is the record made when the root object completes under the current loading criteria, while the latter remains within the snapping track's investigation scope.

Waiting behavior is likewise no longer described as a single synchronous read. `waitForMediaLoaded(world, eid)` yields once per frame until the loader is removed, at which point it ends. Its termination condition is loader removal—not finding the root object visible on a particular frame, nor simply the position no longer changing. To understand the waiting behavior, continue tracing the generator's actual references rather than reducing it to an ordinary query.

On the loading side, the current requirements can be understood in the following stages:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> LoaderAttached
    LoaderAttached --> DescendantsPending
    DescendantsPending --> RootCompleted
    RootCompleted --> LoaderRemoved
    LoaderRemoved --> [*]
```

`LoaderAttached` corresponds to the stage where the loaded object has been attached. `DescendantsPending` preserves the fact that nested descendants still affect the lifecycle. `RootCompleted` indicates that the root object completes only once and that the content boundary is recorded. `LoaderRemoved` is the condition on which termination of the waiting generator depends. The diagram does not show snapping because this loading requirement does not define the snapping fallback object or timing.

## Keep the snapping track separate

`Reversible media snapping` did not automatically acquire complete semantics just because the loading criteria are clear. It still needs to distinguish at least among object position, media reference, and collision shape. Returning to the original position can prove only that the position was restored; only when the media association is seen to be restored can reference restoration be recorded; only when the shape is seen to be handled can shape processing be recorded.

The current decision is not to define snapping recovery as something that necessarily happens after loader removal. Loader removal explains when loading waits end; it cannot therefore specify the snapping workflow, nor determine whether the fallback will read the `mediaRef` and source/file identifiers, or `MediaContentBounds.bounds`. These objects' positions in the loading lifecycle are clear, but they cannot in turn serve as evidence of the snapping implementation.

The page therefore retains a simple working boundary: loading issues begin with actual references to `src/inflators/media-loader.ts`, `MediaLoader`, `MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS`, and `HubsWorld`; snapping issues begin with actual references to `Reversible media snapping`. Only when both sides confirm that they touch the same object or the same point in time should they be written into the same record section.

## Open items still nearby

- How the specific changes in `MediaLoader.count` relate to loader removal still needs to be checked by tracing actual references; this page does not infer the timing of additions or removals from names.
- The identifiers `mediaRef` and source/file already have recording points documented in the loading lifecycle, but there is no conclusion on whether snapping rollback reads them.
- `MediaContentBounds.bounds` is recorded when the root object completes and cannot be directly equated with the collision shape.
- Whether snapping continues to process the same object after the root object completes still needs to be confirmed through references on the snapping side.
- If later evidence is found for only one of position, reference, or shape, add information only for the corresponding object, without marking the other two as restored as well.

These unresolved items do not change the current loading requirements. They define the boundaries of this decision: ancestor counts, the root object's one-time completion, content bounds recording, and frame-by-frame waiting until the loader is removed belong to the loading track; position, reference, and shape restoration in reversible snapping still need further verification through their own references.

## Appendix of Old Examples

**Old example: the root object appears first.**

Early records called this phenomenon "media is complete" and suggested moving immediately to the snapping step. This example is retained as an old example and is no longer used to determine completion. The root object's appearance establishes, at most, an observation of what is on screen; it cannot replace confirmation of unfinished descendants, ancestor counts, or loader removal.

**Old example: the position returns to its original location.**

Early records called this phenomenon "snapping has been restored" and did not go on to document the media reference and collision shape. This example is also retained because it accurately reflects the granularity of observation at the time: the position was observed, but the other objects were not confirmed. It now serves only as a reminder to document position, reference, and shape separately during review.

**Old example: the root node has a completion marker.**

This example came from the old assumption that "the caller will wait for child nodes on its own." That assumption has been withdrawn. A root node marker alone is insufficient to explain the completion of nested descendants, and an unnamed caller cannot be assigned responsibility for waiting without actual references.

The page has evolved from initially listing two names side by side, to retaining two lines of inquiry, to now explicitly defining the loading lifecycle; this is not merely replacing the old wording with a longer version. The old wording conflated visibility, completion, and restoration; the current requirements put loading objects, ancestor counts, root object completion records, and the condition for ending the wait back in their respective places. The snapping track remains on the same page to prevent position restoration from once again being misrepresented as loading completion, not to reach an implementation conclusion for it prematurely.

## R26.9 repair-r1 — authoritative loader ABI clarification

inflateMediaLoader(world, eid, params) accepts src, optional fileId and independent recenter/resize/animateLoad/isObjectMenuTarget/moveParentNotObject booleans. It attaches Networked before MediaLoader and MediaLoading and explicitly initializes count = 0 and mediaRef = 0, including reused entity slots. Count is the number of active loading entries in the loader subtree, including itself: entering MediaLoading increments each MediaLoader on the inclusive ancestor chain once; leaving decrements those same entries once. Inflation itself does not increment. Completion at zero is single-shot after all descendants finish; refresh starts a new lifecycle. mediaRef is the created content eid, initially zero. Source and supplied fileId retain exactly APP.getSid results. MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS values are RECENTER=1, RESIZE=2, ANIMATE_LOAD=4, IS_OBJECT_MENU_TARGET=8, MOVE_PARENT_NOT_OBJECT=16. waitForMediaLoaded(world,eid) is a generator yielding a frame while MediaLoader remains, not a Promise.

# Proposal for Loading Flags and Menu Drops

R26.9: start by discussing loading flags, size constraints, and the object menu's drop action in a single API review. The initial draft's working assumption is to store just one combined state during loading and have the menu read that state when a drop is needed. That would keep the integration surface small, but if resize, recenter, and the loading animation are handled together, callers would have a hard time specifying which one they actually requested.

Two tentative approaches to try.

- Keep separate loading options; apply resizing only when explicitly requested, rather than making it a default side effect of media loading.
- Use a separate target flag for menu drops. It can live on the same object as the loading options, but enabling a visual option should not automatically enter the drop path.

Start with `src/inflators/media-loader.ts`. `addComponent`, `HubsWorld`, `MediaLoader`, and `MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS` appear here, which is enough to anchor this round of discussion; who initiates the drop action and when to clear the target are still undecided.

Also record the withdrawal conditions up front: if independent flags require callers to fill in the entire state again on every load, or if the menu target cannot be stored without interfering with normal media loading, do not keep trying to fit both concerns into the same set of parameters.
versions.change_summary: Recorded the initial direction for separating the concerns and the conditions for withdrawal

# Proposal for Loading Flags and Menu Drops

The initial draft treated "one combined state" as a way to reduce integration costs. After review, that remains an option considered at the time, no longer the default structure. The issue isn't the number of flags, but that different caller intents lose their boundaries in a single true/false check: a load that only asks to recenter shouldn't be reinterpreted because of earlier size settings; nor should the target seen by the menu be inferred indirectly from visual options.

This review follows only `src/inflators/media-loader.ts`. The file shows `addComponent` directly alongside `HubsWorld`, `MediaLoader`, and `MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS`. This shows that the loading entry point touches both component writes and flag definitions, so we can constrain how state is saved here; but it does not show the full sequence of state changes for the object menu. The original draft assigned drop timing to the loader to make discussion easier, not because that ownership had been confirmed.

There are two candidate structures at this point:

| Candidate | State retained | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Combined model | One loading state for sizing, centering, and the menu to read | New options can easily change the meaning of old state |
| Separate-bit model | Each intent is stored separately; the menu reads only target-related bits | Existing callers need to check which bits they actually write |

The preference is for the separate-bit model, but this round does not put the loader in charge of executing menu actions. The loader is responsible for writing persistable loading intent to the component; if the menu needs a target, it should read only explicit target bits. The object menu entry point should still decide whether to perform the drop itself, so that normal loading does not trigger extra actions just because a menu target exists.

The sizing proposal has also been narrowed. What needs verifying here is whether including bounding dimensions in the calculation produces stable results, not adding a scaling strategy for all media. If size information is missing, the candidate approach should retain the original size; don't guess an object's natural size and then write it back to state. This restriction will make some existing callers appear unchanged, but that's easier to debug than persisting an uncertain result.

The next review needs to answer two specific questions: whether existing saved values will be overwritten by the new parameters, and whether the menu must clear its own target bits after completing a drop. If the former requires migrating a large number of callers, the combined model can be reconsidered; if the latter requires the loader to know about the menu lifecycle, the proposal to keep the target bits in the loader should be withdrawn.

# Loading Flags and Menu Drop Proposal

This proposal is still often consulted for the old interface discussion around R26.9, so the wording from the first two rounds has been retained. It records how loading flags and menu drops were once compared side by side; it is not a complete design for object menus. In particular, the first draft's "single combined state" is no longer suitable as integration guidance.

## Disagreements from Earlier Drafts

The first draft was concerned that callers would have to specify options repeatedly, so it proposed bundling recentering, resizing, the loading animation, and the menu target into a single state. That approach seemed to save a few fields per call, but it conflated "this option was not requested" with "this option was saved before." v2 had already downgraded it to a candidate: the combined mode was concise to integrate, but options added later could reinterpret previously saved state.

Another earlier judgment assigned the drop action to the loader. That judgment came from the need for a shared entry point during the discussion; it was not supported by evidence from the surrounding files. That passage is still retained to show why the two topics were placed together at the time; it cannot be used to infer the order of menu actions or decide when menu authorization or cleanup should occur.

## Entry Points Reviewed at the Time

`src/inflators/media-loader.ts` was the original starting point for verification on this page. The file header directly imports `addComponent`, `HubsWorld`, `MediaLoader`, and `MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS`. These direct references narrow the scope to component writes during media loading and the definitions of their flags: this is a place to look when discussing persisted options; discussions of how object-menu drops work still need to return to the actual menu-side entry points.

v2 therefore split the proposal into two questions. The first is how to persist loading intent, with a focus on whether old values and new options can coexist. The second is how the menu identifies a target, with a focus on not reusing the true/false values of recentering, scaling, or animation as the target flag. The two can share state on the same object, but should not share a condition of "do something if any option is set."

| Archived proposal | Rationale at the time | Subsequent treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Combined mode | Compact call interface; easy to integrate initially | Retained as an earlier candidate, not the default recommendation |
| Infer the menu target from loading options | No separate flag needed | Rejected; visual options are not menu targets |
| Persist loading bits independently | Distinguishes each request | Still used; existing bit semantics must be preserved |
| Have the loader perform the drop directly | There was only one shared entry point during the discussion | Not confirmed on this page; investigate on the menu side |

## Current Flag Constraints

This revision corrects bit semantics; it does not add a new menu flow to the loader. The persisted MEDIA_LOADER_FLAGS bits remain recenter=1, resize=2, animate-load=4, and object-menu-target=8; resizing delegates to getScaleCoefficient(0.5, box), and each option composes independently without truthy-default collisions.

This also explains why the combined mode was abandoned: persisted values must distinguish four intents, rather than treating any set bit as a complete loading configuration when read. Resizing still starts with calculating the bounds `box`; it should not be enabled merely because an object happens to have recentering, animation, or a menu target set. Conversely, the menu target is an independent bit; "has resize" or "has animate-load" cannot stand in for it.

Legacy callers that only care about the loading animation can persist just their animation intent; callers that only request recentering do not need to also specify resizing or a menu target. The compatibility cost here is that calls that previously relied on truthiness-based defaults will surface. This change is intentional: treating omitted options as unset is more predictable than guessing that omissions mean a default set of actions.

## Scope Still to Be Trialed

This proposal retains just one boundary for menu drops: they may read the object-menu-target bit to identify candidate targets, but do not have the media loader decide when to execute on the menu's behalf. During the trial, observe three types of input separately: recentering only, resizing only, and menu target only. For each type, the other bits should remain unchanged; then check whether combined inputs still preserve the meaning of each request.

Pay particular attention to bounds information in the resize path. The proposal only requires the existing `box` to be used in the factor calculation; if an entry point has no usable bounds, do not fabricate dimensions and then persist them just to get a visually uniform result. That kind of compensation would hide information missing from the caller and prevent subsequent loads from distinguishing original state from guessed state.

The withdrawal criteria have not changed: if validation finds that independent bits cannot retain their meaning between saving and reading, or that the menu target requires the loader to understand the full menu lifecycle, this split should be withdrawn and the interface placement options compared again. The latter case does not mean restoring the old combined mode as the default; it means moving menu state out of this proposal's loading scope.

A related question still to be worked through: which side clears the target bit after the menu finishes the drop. This page makes no decision; the question remains open because an earlier draft incorrectly described it as an inherent responsibility of the loader.
versions.change_summary: Correct persistence-bit semantics; retain the old proposal

# Media Frame Collision Troubleshooting Tree

The media object looks aligned, but its collision box is offset or has an abnormal size; the object-menu action sometimes doesn't show up. Start with `src/inflators/media-frame.js`.

```text
Offset/abnormal size
├─ guide or bounds are wrong → record media type, per-axis AxisAlignType, scale-to-bounds, stop at the creation section
└─ The above are normal → check the configured extent in kinematic / manual / box
```

The note beside the code now reads: inflateMediaFrame creates the guide and records bounds, accepted media type, per-axis AxisAlignType values, the scale-to-bounds flag, NetworkedMediaFrame and missing Networked state; its kinematic manual box uses half of each configured extent and preserves all-2d as distinct from all.

If collisions are normal and only the menu action doesn't show up, cross-check the configuration closure against HUBS-220; if an item is missing, stop at the corresponding repository file. Don't merge this with the media frame issue. If only entry-point or old-link issues remain, use HUBS-203 to check the page and NetworkedMediaFrame.

# Planar Layers and Inspection Migration Notes

## 2023-06-26 Initial observations

Start by checking two adjacent scenarios around the object menu: one is the planar background and transparent HUD, and the other is the target change after entering inspection. Both appear near the object menu, but the draft has no evidence tying them to the same implementation. During migration, do not mark the inspection flow complete just because the background has been restored.

On the first pass, follow the old path: open the menu and record whether the background and icon appear at the same time; enter inspection and record the current target; if the target can be switched, record one switch in the same scene; finally exit and observe whether the menu still points to the object just checked. The fact that the object remains in world is only an observation; entity existence alone cannot be used to determine the menu state.

## Provisional handling

# Plane Layers and Inspection Migration Notes

This record grew out of a narrow entry point in the object menu. Initially, it covered only the visibility of the plane background; only later were target changes during inspection brought into the same migration path. The page therefore preserves several formulations from different periods: the initial quick assessment, margin reminders written during on-call shifts, a failed recheck that used only a screenshot, an old regression item that was not removed later, and recent verification entry points reconnected from the plane and inspection sides, respectively. They are not a specification written all at once; read them according to where they appear.

## 2023-06-26: First sketch a path that works end to end

Initially, only one test scenario was needed: open the object menu and check whether the background appears; then check whether the icon appears with it; enter inspection and note the current target; if the entry allows it, switch targets once; finally exit. The "seeing" here is an observation from the test run, not a conclusion about the lifecycle. The object is still in world, so this cannot establish that the menu is still using it; the menu disappearing likewise cannot show that the switch did not pass through the old target.

The working hypothesis was brief: for background anomalies, check the plane object first; for state anomalies after exit, check cleanup first. Its purpose was to give the first follow-up investigation a starting point, not to claim that the two phenomena were caused by the same implementation. That version put "restore the background first, then inspect" near the front because it was difficult to observe the icon in the test scenario without the background; the downside was that target switching was hidden in the middle, and later records could not reconstruct which object the menu actually followed.

The draft also retained this sentence:

> First check whether the plane is visible. If it is visible, do not change the rest of the menu; if it is not, switch objects.

This sentence was later shown to be too hasty, but the original text is still worth retaining. It explains why the old troubleshooting process readily replaced the background object directly, and why it left only the "screen restored" result at the time. During migration, it cannot be treated as a completion criterion.

## The First Note Beside the File

The entry was first written as `src/bit-systems/object-menu.ts`. The file header copied at the time was as follows:

```ts
import { addComponent, defineQuery, enterQuery, entityExists, exitQuery, hasComponent } from "bitecs";
import { Matrix4, Vector3 } from "three";
import type { HubsWorld } from "../app";
```

`addComponent`, `defineQuery`, `enterQuery`, `entityExists`, `exitQuery`, and `hasComponent` made it look close to ECS queries and entity checks; `Matrix4` and `Vector3` put menu-object geometry handling near that same file. The note did not go on to list callers, nor infer the complete state machine from import names. The migration investigation still starts from the menu scenario, then compares the actions observed there with the neighboring objects in the file.

This entry point has another practical limitation: the old troubleshooting records were traced from the issue name and call name, but the actual relationship must still be determined by the `v_prev` reference of `internal/HUBS`. A path is enough to help locate the file, but not enough to determine "who creates it, who holds it, and who cleans it up on exit". Earlier versions did not turn this gap into a broader conclusion, and later versions retained this caution as well.

## Summer of 2023: The margin note changed the scene setup

The first margin note required the migrator not to replace the flat-layer screenshot and the inspection screenshot with two completely different scenes. The original scene should first preserve the relationships among the background, icon, and menu layers, and then proceed to inspection. During inspection, first record the current target, then record the target change, and only then record the state after exit. If only entry and exit can be observed, explicitly state that the switching segment is missing; if the target cannot be switched at all in the actual environment, do not use a static image as a substitute.

The margin note also separated the sources of values. When the caller provided no additional choice, record the default path; when the caller had explicitly written a value, record the explicit path. Even if the visuals on the two paths are identical, they must not be merged. What the migration actually changes may not be the color but whether a value is retained or overwritten during object creation. This distinction must also be preserved when rolling back; otherwise, the old path will be obscured by a manually reset default value, and the next comparison will see only the same result.

At the time, the checklist was not long: whether the background appeared, whether the icon appeared, whether the icon covered the background, who the current inspection target was, whether the menu still pointed to the old target after switching, and whether the menu continued to reference the target that had already left after exit. It did not require inventing a new category for every kind of screen, nor did it require including all room entry points in this migration. If any item was missing, the process stopped at that item.

## 2024-06-27: A failed screenshot review

During a second cleanup, the background was replaced with a different flat layer. After the replacement, the background in the screenshot looked normal, so the inspection entry point was going to be run separately again. The problem surfaced quickly: the screenshot did not preserve the original object relationships, so when returning to the inspection menu it was impossible to confirm that this was still the same menu setup; after switching targets, it also did not record the menu's transition from the old target to the new target.

This failure did not mean that the screenshot was completely useless. It could prove that the display had changed at a certain moment, but could not show where the default and explicit values came from respectively, nor whether entry, switching, and exit passed through the same set of states. Thus, the old method was labeled "suitable only for viewing the basic screen" and was no longer used to determine migration completion.

Older records also retained two shorter rules of thumb:

> The background turning black is enough to continue.
>
> The menu disappearing after exiting the inspection is enough to finish.

These two statements are outdated, but must not be erased. The first does not address the icon and the HUD layer, and the second does not address target switching. They show why later revisions added intermediate actions, rather than disguising a misreading of history as if it had never happened.

## Recovery order for the year 2024

After the failure review, the migration sequence was changed to first save the old object relationships, then run through the default and explicit paths separately in the same menu setup, and then enter inspection. On entry, record the current target; when switching, record whether the target changes and whether the menu is still using the previous target; on exit, check whether the menu references a target that has already been left. Plane rendering and inspection remain two separate issue tracks, sharing only the same setup so that a local fix on one side does not obscure differences on the other.

If there is an issue on the plane side, first compare the value sources, then decide whether the plane object needs to be changed. If the background is visible but the icon's stacking relationship is wrong, look instead at the relative order of the icon and background and the layer containing the menu. If there is an issue on the inspection side, first identify whether the change occurs on entry, switching, or exit, rather than lumping all three actions together as "add cleanup on exit". Both issues are near the object menu, but they should not use the same rollback action.

At that point, comparisons across all entry points were still incomplete. A particular entry point might use a different object creation order, but the existing records do not provide a complete call list. This related issue remains open, and conclusions about other entry points cannot be drawn from a single setup.

## 2025-09-23: The plane track has a reproduction entry point again

The records for HUBS-204 brought Plane rendering and transparent HUD layering back into the maintenance steps. The action history first shows that the issue had been reproduced, followed by a move into the handling phase; the public note says that the current workflow covers Plane rendering, but one aspect of transparent HUD remains unconfirmed, with the inputs and outputs kept in the CI shard log. What can be confirmed here is a single reproduction trail and a log location to revisit, and this must not be expanded into a claim that all menu entry points have already been checked.

After this was brought back in, plane-side work no longer just asks "is the background there". In the same object menu, also check whether the icon appears at the same time, whether the stacking relationship between the icon and background has changed, and whether the menu is on the expected UI layer. If the log contains only a particular input and output, use that state as evidence for that specific case; continue to mark transparency behavior that cannot be observed as unconfirmed, rather than using similar colors in a screenshot as a substitute.

Plane migration can be handled separately according to three outcomes: the background value is wrong on the default path, the fields are not retained on the explicit path, or the layering relationship between the background and icon is wrong. These may occur together in a single view, but the entry points for tracing them back are different. When restoring the old path, first revert this round's changes to object relationships, then compare the two value sources again; do not overwrite the explicit fields with default values first.

## 2025-10-21: Restoring the three action stages on the inspection track

The focus of HUBS-221 is an inventory of the current consumers of the Shared ECS inspection lifecycle. The item subsequently completed an interface recheck, then entered review after implementation was completed on the existing branch. The card here provides only inspection-side navigation, without adding a consumer list to this page, or treating review status as a user-visible outcome.

The inspection side needs to record three stages for the same menu. When entering inspection, confirm the current target rather than merely recording that the menu has become visible; when switching targets, confirm whether the target has changed and whether the menu still points to the previous object; on exit, confirm that the menu no longer uses the target just left. The object list can serve as evidence from the session, but an entity's existence does not mean the menu is still using it.

This also corrects the earlier approach of "only checking exit cleanup". The state at exit may be where the symptom appears, but it is not necessarily the cause of the target switch. If there is no observable record during the switch, mark the switch as unconfirmed; if only the switch is visible but the reference relationships after exit are not, limit the conclusion to the observed actions. The plane side is already working normally, but that cannot fill in the missing intermediate states on the inspection side.

## How the old conclusions were crossed out

For the recent recheck, both starting points above must be read in their original time context. "Switch objects if not visible" was the old quick fix; "add cleanup if exit is abnormal" was the old local diagnosis. They have not been retroactively rewritten as correct conclusions, because past commits did in fact follow both of these directions. Now they can only explain earlier changes, and no longer determine the migration steps.

The new verification starts with object relationships, rather than with whether the screen looks good. First retain the pre-migration background and icons, then check the behavior with no additional settings; next check whether the selection explicitly written by the caller is still present; then enter inspection, switch targets, and exit. Each step corresponds to an object or state, and the final screenshot cannot be used to fill in the intermediate actions.

Failures are likewise handled locally. If the background value is abnormal, go back to the values supplied by the plane and the object relationships; if the explicit selection is overwritten, revisit the fields written by the caller; if the HUD order is abnormal, revisit the icons, background, and UI layer; if inspection is abnormal, first distinguish between entry, switching, and exit. If a step lacks evidence, the migration can stop at that step, without borrowing results from other actions.

## Live comparison and restoring the old path

On the first pass before migration, leave the objects unchanged, save only the background, icons, and hierarchy after the menu opens, and record the current inspection target. On the second pass, start with the post-migration object relationships and follow the same sequence:

```text
Open the menu
   ↓
Background and icons → Enter inspection → Record the current target
                            ↓
                         Switch targets
                            ↓
                         Exit inspection
```

"Default" still means that the caller has not provided an additional choice; "explicit" means that the caller has already provided a choice. The two should appear in separate columns in comparisons, even if the visual results are the same. A background appearing only confirms the base scene, not the source of the fields; an icon appearing only confirms that the icon is visible, not the stacking order; a target still existing only confirms that the entity exists, not that the menu is using it.

If the plane migration fails, first restore the plane object relationships changed in this round, retain the original explicit values, and then rerun both the default and explicit observations. If the problem is only with icon overlap, roll back the changes related to the menu hierarchy, and do not change the inspection state at the same time. If the inspection migration fails, restore the entry, switching, or exit handoffs that actually changed, then rerun using the same target sequence. This restores a comparable old path, not a temporary default state that flattens all fields.

If the object menu cannot be opened on site, only record that the entry point is unavailable; if it can be opened but inspection cannot be entered, the plane portion can be retained separately, while the inspection portion stops at the entry point; if inspection can be entered but targets cannot be switched, do not use exit results to fill in target changes. Records for transparent HUD can only cover the portion actually observed or captured in logs, and must not be generalized to other menu entry points.

## Current Plane Behavior

Following the early plane assessments, the margin notes from 2023, the failure reviews from 2024, the old regression checklists, the HUBS-204 reproduction trail, and the supplementary inspection-side notes, the plane behavior that the current migration must preserve is:

inflatePlane and Plane provide the object-menu background with unit opaque-black defaults, while explicit renderOrder, material side, transparency, toneMapped and alphaTest values including zero/false survive; menu icons and backgrounds use deterministic HUD order and the UI layer.

This item comes later to give the current migration work a concrete point of application, not to retroactively supply answers for the earlier historical assessments. During execution, still check in three steps: first confirm the default background path when no additional selection is made, then confirm that fields explicitly supplied by the caller (including values of zero or false) have not been treated as unspecified, and finally confirm that the icon and background use the expected HUD order and UI layer. Do not collapse these three steps into "the colors are correct".

If the default background is not unit opaque-black, first revisit the plane creation path; if the explicitly supplied `renderOrder`, material side, transparency, toneMapped or `alphaTest` are not preserved, revisit field propagation rather than selecting a different background object; if the icon covers the background or the background covers the icon, revisit the deterministic HUD order and UI layer. This only describes the current migration entry point on the plane side, and does not extend it into a conclusion about uniform invocation across all room entry points.

## Current Inspection Criteria

The Shared ECS inspection lifecycle is still checked in terms of entry, switching, and exit. On entry, record the current target; on switching, record the new target and whether the menu has detached from the old target; on exit, record whether the menu continues to use the object you have already left. The object list is used to cross-check the live state, and the entire inspection lifecycle cannot be inferred solely from the results of `entityExists`.

When tracing back through files, still start from `src/bit-systems/object-menu.ts`. The ECS query and entity-check imports at the top of the file indicate that it is close to the query relationships for inspection targets, while the matrix and vector imports from three indicate that it is also close to menu geometry processing. Only when the live actions and the adjacent relationships in the file match should you continue looking outward; do not treat the file's location as the complete call chain.

The completion criteria for the plane side and the inspection side are also separate. The plane side requires, at minimum, actual observations of the background, icon, and layering relationships, with default and explicit sources distinguished; the inspection side requires, at minimum, actual records for all three stages of entry, switching, and exit. A missing stage leaves a gap. The HUBS-204 log entry points only support local verification on the plane side, while HUBS-221 only support dependency navigation on the inspection side, and neither fills in gaps for the other.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Separated Out

For transparent HUD, one state remains unconfirmed and is indicated only by the CI shard log. The current material does not specify which menu entry points this state covers, nor how it relates to inspection target switching. Therefore, if the log can reproduce only the background or a particular icon output, record only that segment; this cannot establish that the transparent layer is stable throughout entry, switching, and exit.

There is also an object-ordering issue on the inspection side: the current material does not provide a complete inventory showing whether different menu entry points all establish the background, icons, and inspection target in the same order. If only one entry point shows a difference later, retain that entry point's object relationships and actions separately, and do not apply a blanket judgment to it based on this page's current flat-layer framing.

Interface verification and review entry points for HUBS-221 are already in place, but the target-switching results users see still need to be compared in the live scenario. The implementation is already complete on the branch, which only means there is an implementation trail available for review; it does not automatically prove that the menu has detached from the old target at the instant of switching, nor does it prove that object references have disappeared after exit.

## Old Appendix: Three-Line Regression Checklist

This regression checklist comes from an earlier record and is retained as-is:

- Open the menu, and continue once the background appears.
- Enter inspection, and continue if the menu remains visible.
- Exit inspection, and finish once the menu disappears.

It covers only the basic visuals, visibility during inspection, and the superficial result after exit. There is no "Switch target" line, nor any source information for default and explicit values, let alone the HUD order of the icons and background. If an old commit contains only these three lines, it cannot be retroactively filled out to serve as the current migration results.

There is also a sentence left beside the appendix: "Inspection and display only need to be stable independently." This no longer applies, because the same object menu still involves state handoffs in actual use. It can help explain why the old regression passed, but it cannot replace the current records of entry, switching, and exit. Do not delete the appendix, and do not write new results back into the old checklist.

## What to Retain at the End of the Migration

Once the flat-layer side is complete, retain before-and-after comparisons of the background, icons, and layering, and mark the observation points for the default path, explicit path, HUD order, and UI layer. Once the inspection side is complete, retain one sequence of entry, switching, and exit, marking the current target after each action. If only the final screen is visible, still record the intermediate actions as unconfirmed.

When the old path needs to be restored, revert the object relationships or state handoffs changed in this round, retain the original explicit fields, and then compare in the same order. Do not first change explicit values to default values, and do not merely add exit cleanup to produce a stable display. Only this way can you retain differences between the old path and the migrated path that can continue to be checked.

# Container Gravity and Hover Troubleshooting Tree

When a media object is in the wrong position in a frozen room, or an object is already pinned but hover remains on screen, first split the observed situation into two records. The first should cover only the offset container, spawner, and gravity behavior after the object appears; the second should cover only the object's hover behavior before and after pinning and before and after pointing at it again. Do not use a single drag to demonstrate both things, and do not combine them into one result just because they both occur in the same room.

The legacy guidance retained on this page is: once the loader completes, attribute any subsequent anomalies to `src/components/media-loader.js`. This entry point was indeed the easiest place to stop during troubleshooting at the time, and media, loader, gravity, group, loaded, and animation on this page are also search terms left over from there. But the legacy guidance turned "you can start looking here" into "the issue must be handled here," and the later review did not provide enough evidence of calls to support it. The tree below is still organized around this entry point to make old samples easier to look up; branches marked as legacy judgments cannot, on their own, establish that a fix is valid.

## Capture the scene first, leave the object unchanged for now

Enter the target room through the user's usual entry point. Before the object appears, note whether the room is frozen, whether the target is already pinned, and whether there is any hover feedback on screen. After the object appears, compare only one thing: position/gravity behavior, or the visible hover state. If the object has not finished being created, do not prematurely record this as a spawner gravity issue; if hover was already present before pinning, do not log it as a phenomenon exclusive to frozen rooms either.

The scene record should answer at least the following four questions:

- Whether the object appeared after entering the room, or a change occurred to an existing object;
- Whether the room's frozen state changed before and after the anomaly;
- Whether hover was already visible before the pin action;
- Whether changes in size or collision shape occurred at the same time as the positional anomaly.

The last item comes from a side note on the old page. The current path shows `computeObjectAABB`, `getBox`, and `getScaleCoefficient` being imported from `../utils/auto-box-collider`, so simply recording size changes alongside position changes makes an old sample more useful than just writing "gravity is wrong." This does not mean collision calculations are the cause, nor does it require checking the collision shape for every hover sample.

## Branch One: offset container and spawner

```text
Position or gravity behavior differs after the object appears
|
+-- Room is not frozen
|   |
|   +-- Stop here: this page does not put differences in ordinary rooms on the frozen-room path
|
+-- Room is frozen
    |
    +-- Anomaly is already present when the object appears
    |   |
    |   +-- Record position behavior before and after spawner creation
    |   +-- Search legacy terms: spawner, gravity, applygravity
    |   `-- Do not change pin or hover state in the same run
    |
    +-- Object initially appears normal, then its position differs
        |
        +-- Record transform before and after offset container involvement
        +-- If size changes too, note the box / scale changes
        `-- Stop: without before-and-after states, do not label this a gravity compatibility issue
```

The legacy procedure treated `mediaoptions.applygravity` as a priority checkpoint. This is retained because it once helped separate gravity samples from ordinary transform samples; it does not guarantee the current processing order. During review, treat it only as a legacy search term: if the scene record does not include gravity behavior, do not fabricate a gravity conclusion just to find this term.

If the object deviates from expectations as soon as it appears, first write down "before spawner creation" and "after spawner creation" as two observation points. Here, "before" does not require inspecting internal state, but refers to the room view before the user entry point is triggered and the first view after the object becomes visible. If any other interaction occurred between these two views, record that interaction and stop attributing a cause. The old page once recommended directly adjusting the group's transform and then checking the result; this would erase the original difference and cannot be the first step in a review.

When an object is initially normal and only shifts later, the old page listed offset container as the only candidate. This branch is still retained because it is the named entry point closest to the topic, but the record must include the stage at which the change occurred: after creation, during the shell animation, or after a room operation. `src/components/media-loader.js` also shows `addAnimationComponents` being imported from `../utils/animation`. If the shift happens to be adjacent in time to the animation phase, you can write "adjacent to animation" in the sample; you cannot use this to conclude that the animation has changed gravity.

If the position difference is accompanied by changes in the object's size, bounding box, or collision shape, the old page required correcting the collider first. This is another legacy judgment that was not fully verified. The correct way to record these accompanying changes is to keep them on the same line, rather than turning them into a new action: for example, "Position differs after the object appears; size changes are also visible." Do not apply this side note to samples without simultaneous changes.

## Branch Two: pinned hover in frozen rooms

```text
hover is still visible
|
+-- Room is not frozen
|   `-- Stop: record this separately as general hover behavior, without applying this page's legacy judgment
|
`-- Room is frozen
    |
    +-- Target is not pinned
    |   `-- Record the conditions under which hover appears; do not label it pinned hover
    |
    `-- Target is pinned
        |
        +-- hover was already present before pinning
        |   `-- Record whether any additional visible changes occur after pinning
        |
        `-- hover appears only after pinning
            `-- Preserve the order of object creation, pinning, and hover; do not change the material or target first
```

The legacy judgment for this line of investigation was even broader: once an object was pinned, any lingering hover was to be treated as a failure. It treated "Pinned hover policy in frozen rooms" as a single visible rule, without distinguishing whether hover already existed before pinning, was newly added after pinning, or the target changed during the process. The legacy judgment remains here because early records used it to filter samples; it does not have enough supporting material to establish that the same conclusion applies to all frozen rooms.

During troubleshooting, first confirm that the room is frozen, then confirm whether pinning was an existing state or resulted from the current operation. If the target is not yet pinned, stop the record at the hover conditions; do not force it into the pinned branch just to match the name. If hover was already present before pinning, compare the visible changes before and after pinning, rather than the single static view of "hover is present." If hover appears only after pinning, preserve at least the order of object creation, pinning, and hover appearance; without that order, subsequent investigators can only reproduce the phenomenon, not determine whether it was triggered by pinning or resulted from switching an existing target.

The old page once recommended recreating the media object whenever hover lingered. That step is now retained as a historical action and should not be done first. Recreating the object changes its creation timing and mixes the spawner branch and hover branch together again. Only after the original view, the states before and after pinning, and the target sequence have all been captured may you start a separate attempt; keep that attempt's results separate from the original sample, and do not overwrite the original record.

## Stopping points when checking `media-loader.js`

After opening the path, look only at names adjacent to the sample, and do not treat the entire file as proof of these two issues. Names left in the old troubleshooting records include media, loader, gltf, group, loaded, transform, animation, gravity, `mediaoptions.applygravity`, and half. They are useful for locating places mentioned in old notes, but they are not a repair checklist to execute in order.

Use the following stopping points:

- If you find code near loader completion but the sample lacks creation timing, return to the scene and add "when the object appears";
- If you find a location related to group or transform but the anomaly manifests only as hover, do not expand the position branch further;
- If you see adjacency to animation but the scene record has no before-and-after views, record only the adjacency to animation, without drawing a causal conclusion;
- If you see the import of auto-box-collider but the sample has no size or shape changes, do not investigate it further;
- When you want to change gravity, transform, and hover at the same time, stop and split the record back into two.

This section is the easiest part of the old runbook to misuse. It originally treated "names can be found near the loader" as "the compatibility boundary has been found." The review did not retain enough actual call chains, nor did it retain results mapping the hover policy to specific loading stages item by item. Seeing a name can therefore only tell you where to look next; it cannot replace the room state, object sequence, and visible changes.

## Review addendum

HUBS-208 serve as navigation entry points for offset container and spawner gravity compatibility; HUBS-225 correspond to pinned hover samples in legacy calls. Both cards later moved into the processing stage, but this page retains no terminal output, CI job, or records from which the outcome can be determined directly. During review, do not substitute card status for the actual scene.

When a sample needs to be handed off, the deliverable should be a short, sequential description, rather than "gravity anomaly" or "hover did not disappear": whether the room was frozen, when the object appeared, whether pinning was already in place, whether the anomaly involved position or visible state, and whether size changes occurred. This lets the next person looking at `src/components/media-loader.js` know which branch to start from, and helps avoid merging the two legacy judgments again.

DOC-20 record another set of checks on spawner creation and delayed shell animation, as well as inspection-wide hover suppression. It can be used to compare terminology, but cannot replace this page's frozen-room samples; the sequence observed in the scene for offset container, spawner, and pinned hover remains the basis here.

Two unresolved points remain: whether the frozen state affects only the branch after the object appears, and whether hover already present before pinning counted as the same type of persistence in legacy calls. The old page had no answers, and the review did not turn them into conclusions either.

# Spawner and Hover Migration Guide

This page originally tracked two compatibility threads together: Spawner creation and delayed shell animation, and Inspection-wide hover suppression. Older troubleshooting typically started with the terms `right`, `remote`, and `held`, entered object-menu, and then followed `object`, `menu`, and `target` to find possible `child`, `load`, `world`, and `transform` relationships.

The working assumption at the time was that the delayed shell animation appearing after Spawner creation completed might be in sync with the object's state changes during creation; Inspection-wide hover suppression, meanwhile, was initially examined based on the local state of the target or child. Neither was finalized as a decision in the initial draft.

```text
Legacy entry
  right / remote / held
          |
      object-menu
       /       \
   target     child

Verification order after migration
  creation -> delayed shell animation
  inspection -> hover suppression
```

The entry currently retained for follow-up checks is `src/bit-systems/object-menu.ts`. At the top of the file, you can see `bitecs`'s `addComponent`, `defineQuery`, `enterQuery`, `entityExists`, `exitQuery`, and `hasComponent`, as well as `three`'s `Matrix4` and `Vector3`; these only indicate the scope of adjacency between the menu object and world transforms and cannot replace checking each location individually.
