# Spawner and Hover Migration Notes

This record began with a very narrow entry point. The earlier investigation did not follow relationships between files, but instead searched for `right`, `remote`, and `held` by symptom names and call names, then grouped the results under object-menu. This quickly located the menu object, but squeezed creation, delayed animation, and hover behavior during inspection onto the same path. During the later review, the focus of the migration was no longer on switching files, but on changing the order of investigation within the file: first check when the object enters the relationship, then check what state remains between the menu and the target, and only then attribute visual changes to creation or inspection.

```text
Path through the old records
  right / remote / held
            |
       object-menu
       /    |     \
  object  target  menu
            |
       child / load / world

Path for review within the file
  creation ----------------> delayed shell animation
       |                              |
       +---- object / child / load ---+

  inspection --------------> hover suppression
       |
  target / menu / transform
```

The actual entry point for verification here has always been `src/bit-systems/object-menu.ts`. The old path left behind declarations within the file and direct adjacencies, which are not enough on their own to account for all callers. The dependencies visible at the top of the file include:

```ts
import { addComponent, defineQuery, enterQuery, entityExists,
  exitQuery, hasComponent } from "bitecs";
import { Matrix4, Vector3 } from "three";
import type { HubsWorld } from "../app";
```

These dependencies explain why the two sets of review material were put together: one side has entity queries and component checks from BitECS, while the other has matrices, vectors, and world objects from Three.js. They do not prove that delayed shell animation is necessarily triggered directly by creation, nor do they prove that hover suppression is determined solely by a particular target flag. The old version presented these two directions as more closely connected, and that framing is retained here to prevent readers from mistaking historical speculation for conclusions from an already completed migration.

## Explanations Retained from the Old Entry Points

The initial draft treated Spawner creation as one continuous action: create the object, attach the child, and wait for the shell to appear. Because entry points were found only by following the relationship terms associated with object-menu, delayed shell animation was temporarily treated as an effect at the end of the creation process. This explanation remains on the page, but it is only an interpretation of the earlier observations, not a description of the current implementation. Without enough material, none of the terms `load`, `world`, or `transform` can be designated as the sole trigger for the animation.

Another earlier explanation narrowed Inspection-wide hover suppression to a single menu target. That narrowed scope has also been left intact. It explains why early checks tended to focus only on `target`: `menu`, `object`, and `child` can all serve as search entry points, and readers entering through any of these terms first see a small set of local relationships. Subsequent reviews should record the actual scope of triggering; the result for one local child cannot stand in for the user path for inspection-wide.

The shared problem with these two earlier explanations is not incorrect names, but treating "finding the file" as "completing the compatibility check". This page therefore retains the old paths alongside the current entry points. To return quickly to the old records, use `right`, `remote`, and `held` to find object-menu; to check the relationships after migration, start by reading the adjacent code for creation, inspection, target, and transform, then check back to see whether the object already exists.

## Review Batches

The first batch covers only the creation path. Start the observation with the object's state before creation, and check whether any additional visible changes occur after Spawner creation completes. Record two things separately: the object has been created, and the shell appears later. Even if both occur around the same frame, that is still no reason to combine them into a single action; if the shell does not appear, do not immediately fall back to "creation failed", and retain the original search terms child, load, and world as well.

The second batch covers the inspection path. First confirm whether the user has entered inspection, then check whether the hover state persists as the menu target changes. Here, "wide" is a scope that needs to be verified, not a conclusion that follows automatically from the local object name `menu`. If the reproduction covers only one object or one target, keep the record limited to that scope rather than presenting it as a result for inspection as a whole.

The same observations must not be used to draw conclusions for both batches. Observations of Spawner creation answer when the object appears and whether the shell is delayed; observations of inspection answer whether hover suppression extends beyond the current target. They can share the object-menu entry point, but compatibility assessments must still retain separate input states and the final observed object changes for each.

## What Was Actually Added to the Timeline

HUBS-209 has an entry classifying the observed scenario on 2025-09-24. By 2025-09-25, the card was back in progress, and the record still noted one unconfirmed point in Spawner creation and delayed shell animation. "File found" has not been written as "migration completed" here; the unconfirmed item remains on this page because it corresponds precisely to the point where the earlier explanation combined creation with the delayed shell.

The record for HUBS-226 later confirmed ownership on 2025-10-29, but this only changed the follow-up path and did not supply user reproduction results for this page. The card still retains a regression item for Inspection-wide hover suppression: trigger this user path using existing tests or examples, then record the parts not yet covered back on the card. This page uses it only for navigation and does not rewrite the card's to-do items as verification that has already happened.

## Migration and Rollback

During migration, retain the old search entry points first, then add local checks within the file. The benefit is that `right`, `remote`, `held`, and object-menu in the old version can still lead readers to the same historical material; new readers can enter through Spawner creation or Inspection-wide hover suppression without first having to guess which object an issue name refers to. Do not turn a migration batch into a full rewrite all at once: first review the creation path to confirm the order of the object and the shell; then review the inspection path to confirm the actual scope of hover.

If a rollback is needed midway through the review, simply return to the old entry points without deleting the old paragraphs. The restoration order is: retain the original searches by issue names and call names, retain object-menu as the destination, and mark again whether creation or inspection remains unconfirmed in the current batch. Do not turn observations of objects, child, or menu targets into final judgments because of a rollback; do not add a statement that an unobserved shell does not exist either. A rollback only retracts the post-migration interpretation, not the observation records.

One earlier practice can easily lead to a mistaken judgment: seeing a change in menu or target and treating it as evidence that the shell animation has completed; another is seeing hover disappear and treating it as evidence that suppression for inspection-wide has taken effect. In both cases, the record should identify what was observed. If all that is known is that `entityExists` or a component query returned a particular state, this still only shows that the local check occurred and does not justify inferring visible animation or cross-target behavior.

## Where to Continue Now

When revisiting Spawner creation, start with entity entry, object relationships, and world-transform adjacencies in `src/bit-systems/object-menu.ts`, and separate "creation completed" and "delayed shell animation" into two observation points. When revisiting Inspection-wide hover suppression, start with target switching during inspection and the relationships between the menu and its targets, and note whether the reproduction extends beyond one target. HUBS-209 is for taking stock of observations on the creation path, and HUBS-226 is for supplementing regression coverage of the inspection user path.

This page remains a stale but referenced migration record. The earlier explanations, old entry points, and unconfirmed items are all retained; only relationships that can be directly checked through this file entry point or the corresponding observations should replace the old paragraphs.

# Video Playback and Interaction Sound Effects Decision

First, retract an early formulation: putting ECS video playback and seeking and Interaction transition sound effects in the same paragraph does not mean they should be covered by the same state description. R26. 9's wrap-up record initially did list the two side by side, and while reading it was also easy to follow the same menu entry and lump playback, position, labels, interaction transitions, and sound into one chain. This grouping was not retained after review.

The May draft left only one narrow decision: trace video by media state and sound effects by configuration closure. Looking back now, that decision is still sufficient, but it did not make clear at the time what it rejected. It rejected the inference that "files are centralized, so state is centralized"; it also rejected writing the display changes after seek and the sound output of transition as actions that necessarily occur in sequence before there were actual references to support that.

The terms retained in the old draft are not a field list. `media`, `ecs`, `video`, `videomenu`, `videomenusystem`, `play`, `pause`, `track`, `head`, `elapsed`, `label`, and `target` are index terms that bring the reading near the video menu. `local`, `networked`, `ownership`, `networkedvideo`, `mediavideo`, and `time` remind reviewers that they cannot determine the handling location for every scenario by looking at only one local menu action. They come from the entry terms of the old investigation; their purpose is to narrow the scope, not to define specific declarations in the code.

There is even less material on the sound-effects side. The known requirement is only to inspect the configuration closure involved in modifying Interaction transition sound effects, and to continue tracing to the corresponding repository file for any missing item. There are no sound parameter names that can be directly reused here, and no conclusions about mixing, devices, or default values. Therefore, this page does not borrow the video's `track`, `head`, or `elapsed` as sound-effect state, nor does it treat media object names as the ownership of sound configuration.

## The Two Filing Approaches Considered at the Time

The first approach was to write one continuous description organized around the menu system. The benefit was smooth reading: starting from `play` or `pause` and reading downward seemed to explain playback, dragging, labels, and interaction transitions at the same time. It would also make each modification appear to require only one entry point. That is also where the problem lies. The video line already has the still-unconfirmed differences among local, networked, and ownership handling; the sound-effects line, however, is concerned with whether the configuration is complete. Merging them first could cause any unconfirmed point to be hidden by the statement that the menu handles everything uniformly.

The second approach was to retain two behavior notes and add the intersection when references were found. The video note records the state, display, and scene differences involved in playback and seeking; the sound-effects note records whether the configuration around transition is closed. A shared file can be a reading entry point without automatically becoming the common responsibility point for both lines. The review adopted the second approach.

This choice does not sever the relationship. The two requirements belong to the same interaction wrap-up and may still meet near the same target, the same transition, or the same menu object. The decision only specifies the recording order: first confirm the objects and references separately, then record the intersection; do not substitute the parallel relationship of the requirement titles for the reference relationship.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> listed
  state "R26.9 parallel listing" as listed
  state "Video: playback / seeking" as video
  state "Sound effects: transition sound effects" as sound
  state "Reference review: video-menu-system.ts" as review
  listed --> video
  listed --> sound
  video --> review
  sound --> review
  review --> [*]
```

The arrows in the diagram show the review order for this record, not the runtime event order. Video and sound effects both return to the same reading entry because the old investigation brought them to `src/bit-systems/video-menu-system.ts` through the issue names and call names; the diagram does not draw this entry as a state owner, nor does it draw either branch as a prerequisite for the other.

## Review of the Entry File

What was added this time is not a complete code walkthrough, but the adjacency relationships visible in the file header. The file directly imports components and query operations from BitECS:

```ts
import { addComponent, defineQuery, enterQuery, entityExists, hasComponent, removeComponent } from "bitecs";
```

It also imports menu or geometry objects from Three.js, as well as numeric and text utilities:

```ts
import { Mesh, MeshBasicMaterial, Object3D, Plane, Ray, Vector3 } from "three";
import { clamp, mapLinear } from "three/src/math/MathUtils";
import { Text as TroikaText } from "troika-three-text";
```

This dependency set changes the reading arrangement from the draft. Previously, searching downward only by requirement name made it easy to treat `play` and `pause` as the only centers; now, component operations, queries, scene objects, rays, planes, and text objects should at least be considered separately. `addComponent`, `removeComponent`, `defineQuery`, `enterQuery`, `entityExists`, and `hasComponent` show that entity- and component-level operations near this entry need to be checked, but they do not themselves specify any particular media lifecycle. `Mesh`, `Plane`, `Ray`, `Vector3`, `MeshBasicMaterial`, and `TroikaText` show that the reading will encounter menu presentation and text objects; likewise, the import names alone cannot be used to infer when labels refresh.

`clamp` and `mapLinear` are also retained as clues for numeric processing. They are worth seeing in related reading about seek, but they do not support treating the range, mapping direction, or boundary conditions as established rules. Earlier records tended to turn "numeric tools exist" directly into "the position has been constrained"; that point is now retracted. Where the actual constraint is, whether it targets the playhead, and whether it also affects the display must be determined from the specific reference.

## Reading Responsibilities After Adoption

The video line starts with the media object. First confirm which object the video menu reads and writes, then distinguish the updates occurring near `play`/`pause` and `head`/`elapsed`, respectively. Only afterward should you check whether `label`, `target`, and the menu presentation objects participate in the same reference. This order is intended to prevent interface text from being treated as a state source; it is not a description of runtime order.

Scene differences are checked at the end of the video line. `local`, `networked`, and `ownership` are kept here because they may change where media state is read or where processing continues. The current record does not group these three into a fixed branch, nor does it assume that a networked object necessarily passes through the local menu. If a reference covers only a local object during review, record only that fact under the local branch; do not add the networked object based on a similar name.

The sound-effects line does not expand from media terms. It starts from the configuration closure involved in the transition modification: first list the configuration locations that have been found, then confirm which interaction transition reads them. If a configuration item is missing, the handling is to continue tracing to the file containing the missing item, rather than temporarily filling the gap with an object or parameter from the video menu. The cost is that one reading pass cannot immediately provide a smooth "click-to-sound" narrative; the benefit is that missing configuration will not masquerade as a playback-state problem.

Once the two lines meet in an actual reference, the intersection record should distinguish at least four things: the object that initiates the transition, the location that reads media state, the location that reads sound configuration, and whether local, networked, or ownership changes the processing location. This is not a new acceptance checklist; it is intended to give later additions fixed places to land. If only one item can be confirmed, write only that item, rather than using the remaining three to complete the story.

## Fallback Wording Not Adopted

One seemingly convenient approach came up in the review: first classify all anomalies as video-menu interaction regressions, then split out the sound portion after confirmation. It was not adopted. This would cause missing sound configuration and media-state anomalies to share the same fault name, causing the investigation record to lose the two different entry points they originally had.

Another approach was the reverse: remove sound effects from this page entirely and retain only playback and seeking. That was not adopted either. The two requirements appear side by side in this wrap-up, and whether interaction transitions are their actual intersection is still worth retaining. Complete separation would force the next review to rediscover this adjacency.

The final choice is the middle approach: make the determinations separately, while allowing them to meet at references. It does not declare module ownership settled, nor does it require future modifications to pass through the same document. If it is later found that playback state and sound configuration are handled by different files, the decision on this page still stands; only the role of the common entry needs to be changed to historical navigation, rather than rewriting the two behavior lines.

## Boundary with the Adjacent Interface Record

DOC-23 contains the interface review for Video gain controls and audio refresh / Held-object cursor scaling precedence. It is adjacent to this page, especially because the term audio refresh may make people assume that it should be folded into transition sound effects. That is not how it is handled currently: the interface issues for gain and audio refresh remain in DOC-23, while this page retains only the history and verification plan for playback/seeking and transition sound effects.

This boundary has a practical purpose. If later reading begins from audio refresh, it should not casually carry the priority of held-object cursor scaling into video-state determination; if it begins from held-object cursor scaling, it should not infer the source of transition-sound configuration in the reverse direction. The two documents can cross-navigate, but each retains its own decision scope.

## Outstanding Review Items

- After `play` or `pause`, do `head` and `elapsed` read from the same state source;
- Does `label` after seeking depend on `target`, and is this target the same in local and networked scenarios;
- When ownership changes, which object continues to process media state;
- Can the configuration closure for transition sound effects stand independently of video actions;
- Do missing sound-configuration items and video-side state anomalies ultimately land in the same reference, or do they land in different files;
- If interface-level gain or audio refresh information is needed, should the addition go in DOC-23 or in this page's intersection section.

This review retracts the early statement that "the same entry point means the same chain," while retaining the draft's core arrangement: read video state and sound configuration separately; only write their intersection back into this record when actual references support it.

# Linked Media Hold resolution Migration Guide

This review initially had a very narrow entry point: the old investigation record traced the issue name and call name to `src/components/media-loader.js`. At the time, it was easy to mistake "the path was found" for "the relationship had been fully explained." During the later review, this entry point was retained, but the work was split into two things: whether the wording about Hold resolution in the release materials still applies to linked media; and which objects around the media loader need to be checked again, which must not all be migrated just because they appeared in the same investigation section.

The starting point for HUBS-214 was a result regression after a Hold resolution upgrade. The card's to-do did not call for changing the runtime implementation; it called for checking the current wording in the release notes, user documentation, and templates, and listing the specific files to change. Therefore, "migration" here first means locating the old wording at each occurrence, confirming what object it refers to, and then scheduling its replacement; it is not a blanket cleanup of all media interaction.

## Preserve the old materials first

The initial draft treated the media loader as the sole checkpoint. That judgment was too strong, and it is still retained here to avoid repeating the mistake. `src/components/media-loader.js` is the code re-check entry point, not an index of the release materials, and it cannot by itself establish which component hover, pen, sound, or scaling belong to.

The first round of collection follows material locations, not guessed behavior:

- For paragraphs in the release notes that mention Hold resolution, save the original sentence, the neighboring heading, and the sentence planned for replacement;
- For user documentation that mentions holding, linked media, or media controls, record who it says is operating and what object the operation affects;
- If a template contains copyable interaction text, record the template name, the existing placeholder text, and what category of page it will flow to;
- If the same text discusses both ordinary media and linked media, do not immediately split it into two new rules. First mark whether the original text already distinguished these two objects.

What needs to be preserved here is readable material from before and after the migration, rather than changing every occurrence into the same sentence pattern. Release notes can simply summarize a change; user documentation explains the operation; templates carry the text to new pages. Even if all three mention the same term, they do not necessarily need to be changed to the same sentence.

Do not delete the original sentence outright before the wording has been confirmed. The migration record should retain at least: the material category, the paragraph location, the old wording, the proposed wording, whether it explicitly points to linked media, and whether the basis for the determination came from a code re-check or manual reading. This way, if someone discovers that an old usage is still used by a compatibility caller, the original occurrence can be restored without rolling back the entire batch of changes.

## The code entry only answers local questions

After opening `src/components/media-loader.js`, first inspect the local adjacency of the media loader itself. The two dependencies visible at the file header are worth using as re-check anchors:

```js
import { computeObjectAABB, getBox, getScaleCoefficient } from "../utils/auto-box-collider";
import { addAnimationComponents } from "../utils/animation";
```

The first line indicates that the file is adjacent to the automatic bounding-box tool; the second indicates that it is also connected to the animation component. They are enough to remind the reviewer not to search only for the term Hold resolution: if a change passes through the media loader, confirm whether it touches the parameters, initialization order, or post-generation state of these adjacent objects. Conversely, these imports themselves do not prove that the automatic bounding box or animation should be adjusted as part of this copy migration.

Keep the re-check order simple:

1. Locate processing in the media loader adjacent to linked media, media visual objects, or hold state;
2. Record the actual call names or data fields seen; do not turn words from the issue title into code facts;
3. If the processing continues into the automatic bounding-box or animation tools, follow it there to see whether the call is merely a shared step in the loading phase;
4. Only when a piece of processing can be linked to the target object described by the copy should it be written into this migration's change description;
5. Keep adjacent items that cannot be linked in the record as "reviewed, not included in this batch"; do not bring them into the release notes because their names are similar.

This sequence is not about finding every caller; it prevents copy changes and local code reading from being mistaken for each other. For compatibility callers, the record should clearly state which confirmed location it enters the media loader from, whether it handles linked media, and whether it still uses the scenario described by the old wording. Until the list has been compiled, do not provide speculative names.

## Do not submit the three material batches together

Release notes, user documentation, and templates are best handled in separate batches. That way, if one batch finds that the original wording is still in use, that batch can be stopped without affecting the location work for the other two categories.

**Release notes batch.** First confirm whether the text describes the result of an upgrade or promises current behavior. The former can retain a historical tone, with the applicable scope for linked media added only where necessary; the latter must wait until the code re-check is complete before being replaced. If a note mentions only ordinary media, do not unilaterally broaden it just because linked media appeared in the same version.

**User documentation batch.** The main thing to avoid here is presenting "holding" as a generalized operation. Check whether the original text already states that the object is linked media, whether it puts the visual result and the control result in the same sentence, and whether it references template text. Mark user-documentation changes locally first; do not share a paragraph of new copy with the release notes, because their readers and temporal contexts differ.

**Template batch.** The risk with templates is their propagation scope. A hold description in one template may be used on multiple media pages, so before replacing it, first mark whether it contains linked-media-specific wording. If this cannot be confirmed, keep the old template and only create a location to be changed; do not write an unconfirmed scope just to make all three batches finish at the same time.

At the end of each batch, a short one-line result is enough, such as "Found two occurrences of the original wording; the second is still awaiting re-check" or "The template has synonymous wording, but the object is unclear." Do not treat the number of located occurrences as a compatibility conclusion. When restoration is actually needed, roll back by batch: first restore the original sentences replaced by that batch, then retain the search locations and re-check notes, so that the restoration does not also wipe out materials that have already been confirmed.

## A separate check for linked media

The scope of this task is limited to linked media. During the check, select existing related pages or template fragments, first confirm where the copy referenced on the page comes from, and then return to the media loader to check whether that object passes through the entry currently being inspected. If the page material only says "media" and does not explicitly mention linked media, list it as having unclear scope and do not use it to support broadening the scope.

The following small diagram can be used to arrange the manual check. The arrows indicate the order of reading and recording, not runtime call relationships:

```text
Old issue trail
    |
    v
src/components/media-loader.js ----> Local adjacency: auto-box-collider / animation
    |
    v
Known linked media page or template
    |
    v
Release notes ── User documentation ── Template
    |                    |
    +------ Confirm in batches ----+
             |
             v
        Keep or replace the original wording
```

The "Keep" in the diagram does not mean abandoning the work. It means that the current evidence supports only leaving one piece of wording unchanged and recording the reason in the migration record. For items confirmed to need replacement, reread the entire paragraph containing the item after making the change, rather than checking only whether the new term appears; this can reveal cases where the original paragraph mixed ordinary media with linked media.

If the same page contains both a visual description and a media-control description, check them separately. The visual description may simply be the presentation after loading, while the control description may involve hold state; even when they are close together on the page, they cannot be treated as the same compatibility commitment. This distinction is especially applicable to templates, because templates often retain only short phrases, making it difficult to tell which object they point to once they are out of context.

## Later review records

HUBS-214 initially had a baseline record, followed by one assignee change. During the later review, a public comment described the scope to review as: "In the Hover, hold, pen, sound, and scaling systems section, one point concerning Hold resolution for linked media remains unconfirmed." This reminder should be understood as written: it identifies one additional unconfirmed point in the same review section and does not combine the five adjacent systems into one change.

Therefore, this page covers only the portions related to Hold resolution and linked media. hover, pen, sound, and scaling can serve as context labels when reading the code and help locate that work area; if they need independent conclusions, they should each have their own record. Writing them into the release notes or user documentation would make readers think that this migration already covered all interaction regression.

The relationship with DOC-26 should also remain at the navigation level: it records the validation design for Bidirectional media mirroring. The two pages can use the same media sample to reduce duplicate setup, but do not put mirroring observations here, and do not use this page's copy-check results to replace the validation record there.

## Status to leave before submission

The card's check items for the current wording of the release notes, user documentation, and templates should still be marked one by one; do not substitute "read the media loader" for completion. Every change prepared for submission should include at least the original material location and the determination of its object; every item not being changed for now should include one sentence explaining why it is on hold. This way, if a regression appears later, it is possible to first check whether old copy is still circulating, whether the template has expanded the scope, or whether the actual processing near the media loader is inconsistent with the wording.

If any of the following occurs, stop replacement for this batch and restore the old path: the original paragraph does not distinguish ordinary media from linked media; the code re-check finds no processing that supports the new scope; the template's adoption scope is unclear; or a compatibility caller still depends on the scenario described by the old wording. When restoring, revert only the wording changed in this batch, while retaining the original sentence, the candidate replacement, and the reason it remains unconfirmed. Continue the next round from these records; there is no need to relocate the issue again from the issue title at HUBS-214.

The current verification entries remain `src/components/media-loader.js` and HUBS-214. The former is used to check local implementation adjacency, and the latter is used to track the unfinished checks for the release materials, user documentation, and templates.

# Quality Signal Console Window Checklist

At the end of the window, check the current entry point first; don't work backward from cleaned-up results to infer the original state. This records the borrowing, output, return, and rollback actions for this react components · Quality Signal Board window; build queues and release steps for other projects are not included.

The previous short note only said not to clear the state after seeing compatibility path. That wasn't enough when the records from both sides were later compared: records with the same name can come from different generation commands and can also date from different times. The HUBSA-008 check therefore stops at the first divergence, rather than picking a newer output and continuing to interpret from there.

## What to retain when opening the window

- [ ] Record the current entry point and the version actually used. `docs/adj-react-components/release/react-components-quality-signal-board-short-checklist-before-window-end.md` remains the authoritative entry point.
- [ ] Retain the original input, the first visible result, and the final output. If a later rerun changes the state, mark it separately; do not overwrite the first result.
- [ ] Keep one successful sample from the project itself and one rejected sample. These are only for determining whether this Quality Signal Console window remains within its original boundaries.
- [ ] Record what was borrowed, who is using it, and when it will be returned. Do not proceed to the window-closing steps if a borrowed item has no return time.

HUBSA-007 require clearing your own cache and rerunning the current entry point; shared caches are outside the scope of this checklist. First save the output from before the cleanup, then clear the local cache, then run the same entry point once more. If the post-cleanup result differs from the original record, just save the differences side by side; do not immediately label either one the final result.

HUBSA-008 require comparing the generation commands and times of the two Quality Signal Console records. Use this fixed comparison order: commands first, then times, then the first point of mismatch. The first mismatch is the stopping point. Even if later lines appear to match, do not use them to smooth over this divergence.

## Window-closing steps

- [ ] The last output has been saved and can be matched to this window's current entry point.
- [ ] If a local cache rerun was performed, the original output and rerun output can still be distinguished.
- [ ] Borrowed items have been returned; if not, record a new latest return time and keep the window open.
- [ ] The rollback entry point is documented and confirmed to be for this change to adj-react-components, not an entry point for an adjacent project.
- [ ] Unresolved divergences, sample gaps, or recovery questions remain in the original record; do not delete them just because the window is being closed.

The old-version image has already been removed; recovering that image must not be a prerequisite for this check. Any comparison that needs it to continue stops at "historical version unavailable"; retaining the existing outputs, commands, and times is enough. Do not substitute another image just to complete the comparison, or treat a substitute as the old version.

## Stopping and rolling back

Stop closing the window and preserve the state if any of the following occurs: scene entry is missing; the two records show their first divergence in generation command or time; a local cache rerun changes the first result; a borrowed item has no return time; the rollback entry point cannot be confirmed.

When rolling back, undo only the borrowing and temporary changes introduced by this window's current entry point, then check again that the last output is still in its original location. If the rollback itself changes the result, record both the pre-rollback and post-rollback outputs; do not overwrite either one. There is still no usable sample for restoring the shared environment; keep this as an open item.

HUBSA-007 and HUBSA-008 provide navigation only for this rerun and divergence check. For the record of the trade-off between the cache and the original state, see DOC-32.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Window Checklist

Closing the window does not end with simply saving a green result. On the Quality Signal Dashboard side, an output often looks normal at first, only for someone to discover later that it came from the local cache after cleanup, or that the records on the two sides were not generated in the same run. Before the window ends, preserve the entry point used at the time, the original input, the first visible result, the final output, and when borrowed items are returned. Keeping these together lets the next person taking over distinguish between "this run worked" and "the state has already changed".

This record retains the original scope: it covers only borrowing for the current entry point, the final output, the return time, and the rollback entry point for adj-react-components. It does not take over the entire release process or replace build or artifact assessments outside the Quality Signal Dashboard. The entry file is still `docs/adj-react-components/release/react-components-quality-signal-board-short-checklist-before-window-end.md`. Matching filenames do not mean that two outputs were generated in the same run; when closing the window, record both the actual entry point and the version you are looking at.

The early checklist contained only one narrowly scoped reminder: do not clear the existing state after seeing compatibility path, and stop if scene entry does not appear. This reminder remains because it still prevents a missing entry point from being mistaken for a completed path. However, it did not address caching or the time difference between two records. Later notes have separated these two gaps: first verify cold-start differences at the current entry point by rerunning with the local cache cleared; when the records on the two sides differ, first compare the generation commands and times, and stop at the first divergence. Do not treat a few later lines that happen to match as evidence that the divergence has disappeared.

## Records Before Opening the Window

- [ ] Write down the current entry point and version used this time. The record must let someone return to the same entry point, rather than merely saying "Quality Signal Dashboard has run".
- [ ] Preserve the original input. Once the input has been cleaned up or replaced, subsequent output can no longer show the conditions under which it was obtained.
- [ ] Preserve the first visible result. Even if the first result is a failure, do not overwrite it with a later green result; failure samples are the starting point for assessing regression stratification and attributing unstable signals.
- [ ] Preserve the final output from this run. It may be a success, a rejection, or an interruption; what matters is that it can be matched to the current entry point, the original input, and the execution order.
- [ ] Record the borrowed items and their return deadlines. Without a return time for a borrowed item, the window cannot be considered to have entered the closing stage.
- [ ] Write down the rollback entry point for adj-react-components in the same place. The rollback entry point must be distinguishable from the current entry point for this run; an operation with the same name in a neighboring project cannot be used as a substitute.

Keep one "success sample" and one "rejection sample", but do not repeat runs just to fill the sample set. The success sample confirms that the current entry point has produced the expected path; the rejection sample confirms that this operation has not swallowed the boundary. Preserve both in their first visible form. If the same input first produces a rejection and later a success, preserve both in chronological order, without using the second to invent an explanation for why the first failed. This step only checks whether the records are complete; do not expand it into a new attribution exercise during window closure.

Apply the same principle to borrowing. The window-closing record should show what was borrowed, when it was still in use, and when it must be returned. Do not merely write "handled" or "will return later". If the return time cannot be determined, keep the window open; if the borrowed item has been returned, preserve the location of the final output before its return, so that no one has to guess what was seen after the borrowed item has been removed. Returning an item does not mean deleting its traces; instead, it requires keeping the final output somewhere it can still be reviewed.

## Cache Check for the Current Entry Point

The scope of HUBSA-007 is to clear your own cache and rerun the current entry point once; leave the shared cache untouched for now. This restriction must not be omitted. The shared cache is not something you can casually clear to compare cold-start differences in this check; once you touch it, the boundary between the original state and the local rerun disappears as well.

Follow this order:

1. First save the original input, current entry point, first visible result, and final output from before clearing the cache. If this step is incomplete, do not clear the cache yet.
2. Confirm that you are clearing your own cache. Stop if there is no clearly defined scope for operations on the shared cache; do not continue on the grounds that "we can rerun it anyway".
3. After clearing the cache, start from the same current entry point. Do not use this rerun to switch entry points, switch to a similar test path, or bring in another output along the way.
4. Save the rerun result alongside the result from before clearing the cache. Record the order in which they appeared; do not overwrite the original location with the rerun result.
5. If the two results are the same, simply preserve that fact; it shows that this local-cache rerun did not change the observed result, but it does not replace checking the generation records on both sides.
6. If the two results differ, stop the remaining window-closing steps. First preserve the difference as a sample of an unstable signal from the Quality Signal Dashboard; do not use this checklist to choose which result is more trustworthy.

A green result from a local-cache rerun does not justify deleting the initial failure sample. On the contrary, when green and failing results coexist, that is precisely when the original input, first result, and rerun result need to be preserved. If someone has already kept only a cleaned-up output, restore whatever original records can be found; if they cannot be restored, state the gap explicitly, and do not present the cleaned-up green result as the only record of the state at the time.

This does not require a conclusion for every difference. The Quality Signal Dashboard has follow-up work on regression stratification and attribution of unstable signals, but before the window ends, all that is required is to preserve samples that can be checked. When there are not enough samples, stopping at the gap itself is better than filling the record with explanations. In particular, do not interpret a single rerun after clearing the cache as proof that all tests are stable, and do not mark the current entry point as unusable because of a single rejection.

## When Two Records Do Not Match

HUBSA-008 points to the case where two react components · Quality Signal Board records do not match. Start the check with the generation commands and times, not with which output looks more like the right answer. Preserve both sides unchanged and compare them in the following order:

1. Retrieve the generation commands from both records. If the commands differ, record the difference directly as the first divergence; do not continue overwriting one result with the other at this point.
2. If the commands match, check the generation times. If the times differ, first record their chronological order, then treat the point where the times differ as the first divergence.
3. Only when neither the commands nor the times show a difference should you examine the outputs item by item for the first mismatch. Stop as soon as you find it; do not include later content that happens to match in the assessment.
4. Content after the first divergence may be kept as an attachment, but it does not change the stopping point. The window-closing record only needs to identify the shared portion before the divergence and the location where the divergence occurs.

The purpose of this step is not to select the "correct record", but to prevent material from two different sources from being merged into one when the window closes. If the commands differ, matching subsequent output does not make them the same generation run; if the times differ, the later record does not automatically replace the earlier one. If the divergence needs further explanation, preserve the generation commands, times, and outputs from both sides, and pause the window here.

Handle cases where an old-version image has already been cleaned up separately. When the old version cannot be obtained, do not describe finding a similarly named substitute as restoration. What can be preserved from the existing material is the generation commands, times, original inputs, and outputs at the time for both records; explicitly mark the missing old image as unavailable. Questions that depend on the old image remain unresolved and cannot be overwritten by a new generation run. This restriction also applies to local-cache reruns: they can only show what the current entry point looks like after this cleanup, and cannot recover historical versions.

## Check Each Item Before Closing the Window

- [ ] The current entry point and version have been recorded, and the entry file can still be located.
- [ ] The original input, first visible result, and final output have been saved separately.
- [ ] One success sample and one rejection sample have been preserved, without being replaced by output cleaned up later.
- [ ] If a local-cache rerun was performed, the results from before and after clearing the cache have both been preserved, with their order stated explicitly.
- [ ] The shared cache was not cleared for this cold-start check.
- [ ] If the two records do not match, their generation commands and times have been compared, and the check stopped at the first divergence.
- [ ] Any unavailable old-version image has been retained as an explicit gap, without passing off a substitute as the original.
- [ ] If a borrowed item is still present, its return deadline has been recorded; if it has been returned, the final output can still be reviewed.
- [ ] The rollback entry point has been confirmed to belong to this window for adj-react-components.

If any item cannot be checked off, do not declare the window closed. Leave the reason next to the corresponding item: whether scene entry is missing, the original input is absent, the first result was overwritten, the cache rerun changed the result, the records first diverge at the command or time, the old-version image is unavailable, or a borrowed item has not yet been returned. The reasons do not need to be compressed into one generic status; preserve the specific gaps so that the next person taking over knows where to continue.

## Stopping and Rolling Back

Stop in the following cases: scene entry has not appeared; the current entry point cannot be confirmed; the result after clearing the local cache differs from the original result; the two records show a first divergence in their generation commands, times, or outputs; a borrowed item has no return time; the rollback entry point cannot be confirmed; continuing the check requires an old-version image that has already been cleaned up.

When stopping, do not clear the existing state, delete failure samples, or turn incomplete items into "passed". Preserve the last confirmed output and state where you stopped. If you stopped at a cache difference, preserve both outputs from before and after clearing the cache; if you stopped at a divergence between records, preserve the commands, times, and first difference on both sides; if you stopped at borrowing, preserve the borrowed item and its return time. This ensures that rollback and subsequent checks do not have to start from a blank slate.

Rollback only handles borrowing and temporary changes introduced by the current entry point in this window. Before rolling back, confirm that the final output has been preserved; after rolling back, check whether the entry point can still be located. If the rollback action itself changes the result, keep the outputs from both before and after rollback; do not rewrite the state observed during the window using the post-rollback state. If the rollback entry point cannot be independently confirmed, stop before confirmation rather than substituting an operation from another project.

HUBSA-007 has entered the handling stage, but this does not change the stopping points above. Work having started only means that the current entry point needs further follow-up; it does not mean that cache differences, record divergences, or gaps in historical images have disappeared. HUBSA-008 remains the navigation entry point when two records do not match; for the trade-off between the cache and the original state, see DOC-32. After completing the window-closing record, preserve this window's input, output, return, and rollback records, and append the next window starting from a new version without overwriting this round's unchanged original material.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Cache Trade-off Record

The earliest entry on this page recorded a narrow choice: react-components-quality-signal had a current revision that was still usable at the time, but rebuilding the environment would rework the original setup. The debate was not about whether to make the quality signals more complete, but about which layer the record should preserve.

The two initial options

Continuing with `physics shape` would minimize changes to the existing entry point. It keeps structure and results in the same place, making them easy to look up, but the cleaned-up green state can obscure the original failure state. The other option was to separate out `release trace`; this would preserve a path that was actually taken, but would require readers to understand both the old entry point and the new record. The sample would also be narrower in the short term.

During review, someone insisted on staying with the old entry point. The reasons were specific: the existing page could be opened, the current revision did not need to be prepared again, and we should not introduce another environment difference just for the record format at that stage. This view remains on record because it concerns maintenance cost, not a rejection of `release trace`.

The decision recorded at the time was to capture only one real usage path and not rebuild the environment at that stage; `world tick` would not change as a result of this adjustment. `entity lifecycle` was retained as a counterexample: it shows that a single path cannot represent all interactions, but was not enough to justify a full split. This record did not mark the callers of `object list` as confirmed, nor did it promise that a rollback would restore only the old entry point.

Observations added later

The record for HUBSA-002 had, by 2025-11-24, already been classified as failure_classified. By 2025-11-28, a public comment on the card noted: the expiry action was no longer valid, and the entry-point guidance on the page had not been updated. This meant that "the old entry point still opens" no longer implied that the entry point was still accurate; the access preserved by the cache and the next step the page showed users had diverged.

HUBSA-003 recorded qa_reproduced on 2025-12-01. Another public comment was more limited: after switching to a different account or workspace, it got as far as the logout entry point and stopped. This result did not prove that all usage paths failed; it only showed that under different conditions, the logout action still needed to be examined as a separate case. Nor did it fill in the missing caller information for `object list`, so the original open issue remained.

These two records changed the balance of the trade-offs; they did not retroactively turn the initial decision into a mistake. Continuing to use the current revision still avoids the additional differences introduced by rebuilding the environment, but the record must not preserve only the cleaned-up state. When using a single path, the `release trace` encountered along that path must be preserved alongside the original state. In particular, "the entry-point guidance has not been updated" must not be used to infer that the logout action has completed.

Handling of rejected options

We did not choose to move all interactions directly to `physics shape`, nor to collect all `entity lifecycle` in one go. The former would continue to mix the original state with the cleaned-up results; the latter would require more real consumers and go beyond the material available for this decision. `content bounds` and `raycast state` can still serve as lookup terms in the observations, but must not be used to infer unrecorded call relationships.

Therefore, two things remain in place: first, continue using the current revision without rebuilding the environment for this page; second, capture a separate `release trace` using one real usage path and retain its corresponding original state. The scope of a single path must not be extrapolated to the whole of react components · Quality Signal Board. HUBSA-002 and HUBSA-003 serve only as pointers to the later observations, leading respectively to the record of the invalid entry-point guidance and the record of stopping at the logout entry point; they have not replaced this decision.

Rollback remains scoped to individual parts. First distinguish between the old entry point, the cached content, and the logout action, then determine which item needs to be restored; do not mark the entire path as restored just because one state has returned to its old value. If new real consumers emerge later, or the callers of `object list` are confirmed, create a new version to record the change in scope. This version does not record future implementation work as completed.

# Dependency Boundary Record Divergence Postmortem

This wasn't a case of lost records: the same entry point retained two revisions, both as the current revision. When readers opened it, they would first see an old record that was still treated as the current conclusion, while linked media pointed to a different set of content. There was no note reconciling the two and no clear indication of which assessment should continue to be used.

The earliest sign was a mismatch between linked media and the old record. The assessment at the time was that the attachment replacement was incomplete, so we first followed the old record to check the entry point more closely. That assessment did not fully hold up: both sets of material were still readable at the entry point itself. The problem was that they had been placed side by side without any indication of which came first.

## Timeline

- When we first checked, the scope of adoption stated in the old record was still at the top of the entry point, making it easy for readers to treat it as the only version.
- We then found material from another revision at the same entry point. It had not replaced the old assessment; it had simply been left right beside it.
- After comparing the two sets of material, we decided not to keep retrying the merge. We left `docs/adj-utils/incidents/utils-dependency-boundary-audit-two-version-records-not-merged.md` exactly as it was at the time, to avoid collapsing the differences we had already seen back into a single unverified conclusion.
- The review could only confirm that loader ancestry could be traced back to two sources. That explained why the material could still be found, but not why ownership handoff had changed.

The main impact was on adoption decisions. Readers who saw only the entry point might continue to rely on the old record to understand the dependency origins established by lock and license; readers who saw linked media would get a different current revision. There was no clear replacement relationship between the two sets of content, so they could not establish which one actual consumers had adopted, nor could the entry point be used to infer that exit responsibility had changed.

Keeping the old record at the time was intentional: the old assessment had indeed been shown at the entry point, and deleting it outright would have removed the starting point for later comparisons. But the claim that "as long as the entry point still opens, the old record can still serve as the current basis" was no longer reliable. It only showed that the old material was still there, not that it was still being used.

DOC-37 can be read as adjacent records in the migration index, but the two pages are not combined into a single conclusion here. This page records only the side-by-side state observed this time and the decision to stop retrying.

Still missing from the timeline: when the two revisions came to coexist at the entry point, and at which step ownership handoff changed. If read results from actual consumers become available later, append them after the old assessment without overwriting the side-by-side state observed this time.

# Compatibility Directory: On-Call Runbook for Failed Runs

When you take over a run, preserve the first state you see before deciding whether to continue. The entry point is fixed at `docs/adj-systems/runbooks/systems-compatibility-catalog-one-failed-run-on-call-page.md`, and the object is this project's `systems-compatibility-catalog`. Don't refresh permissions, restart, or recreate data just because the page appears to show an old state; those actions will make it impossible to compare against the first result.

The sequence in the old record is still useful, but it only tells you how to find the first difference: after opening the object, look at `entity lifecycle`, then `menu target`, and finally confirm `network state`. The old record does not establish that recovery succeeded, so don't treat it as a pass criterion while on call.

## Preserve the Run State First

At the entry point, record:

- The object actually being handled and the path used to access it;
- The object's current version and the state shown on the page;
- The original input, the first visible result, and the time the result appeared;
- Actions already taken.

First, save the input and the first result as they are. If the same object shows two states, record each one; don't overwrite the earlier state with the later one. If you can't yet confirm that the object is `systems-compatibility-catalog`, stop at the entry point; don't substitute a similar object.

## Check in the Order Observed

Go to `entity lifecycle` first. Record only states that have already appeared here; if part of the sequence is missing, leave the gap. If the entry point itself won't open, record the entry point, object, and first error, and stop further attempts. Don't skip ahead to the menu or network steps.

Once you can confirm the lifecycle, check `menu target`. If it has already appeared, save the page or output as it was then; don't delete actions, clear the run state, or recreate the input. The on-call goal is to preserve the first failure point, not to make the page look normal again first.

Next, wait for and check `network state`. If it doesn't appear, stop at this step and save the original input, page state, and object version. Without a new result, don't record that the network has recovered, and don't create another run by refreshing, restarting, or changing permissions.

If `network state` appears but the menu result still differs from the reference sample, stop at the menu difference and record only what changed in this comparison; don't attribute the difference directly to the network. If you only saw `menu target` and no network state, this is still an incomplete run; don't proceed to recovery actions.

## Handle Each Branch

First difference occurs before `entity lifecycle`: include only the entry point, object, and first result in the handoff; leave the next step to someone who can access that entry point.

First difference occurs in the middle of the lifecycle record: preserve the missing window; don't fill it with later states. When a state reappears, still record the two states on either side of the gap separately.

Menu has appeared, network state is missing: stop this attempt at the network check and save the originals before exiting. If you later want to try recovery, first make a separate note of the single condition you plan to change and the results to compare.

Entry point, object, or first difference cannot be matched up: don't continue with rollback. Preserve the run state first and note which item is missing so you don't merge in another run.

## Recovery and Rollback

Recovery actions have not yet been validated in the shared environment. Finding the entry point does not mean the run has recovered; record "entry point found" and "recovery result observed" separately in the handoff. If a recovery test changes conditions, you must also retain the input and first result from before the change.

Only attempt rollback if you have retained the pre-change originals. First verify the object and entry point for the rollback, then perform the return action and make a new record of the first visible result after rollback. If pre-change records are missing, or you can't confirm which object the rollback applies to, stop at verification; don't reconstruct the run state from memory. A normal state after rollback must not overwrite the original failure record either.

## Handoff Record

When the next shift takes over, use the path above to enter and read the original run state first. The handoff must include at least the specific object, entry point, object version, original input, actions already taken, first failed step, first result, rejected hypotheses, and next check time. Leave any assessment without new evidence as originally worded; don't rewrite it as a conclusion confirmed today.

Still unanswered: whether recovery actions in the shared environment will change the original menu result, and whether `network state` will appear at the same entry point after rollback. Keep these as open items until they have been verified.

# Compatibility Directory Window Checklist

This checklist covers only four things to check before the window ends: borrowing the current entry point, the final output, the return time, and the rollback entry point for adj-systems. It captures the wrap-up sequence used at the time, not release decisions that are not listed here; anything not listed still needs confirmation from the original owner.

## Before the Window Ends

1. Open `docs/adj-systems/release/systems-compatibility-catalog-short-checklist-before-window-end.md` and first look for `loader ancestry`. Verify that the current entry point is still the one borrowed for this window, then save the final output in the same record. If the entry point name does not match, the output points elsewhere, or only the old entry point is visible, do not continue cleaning up the setup; leave it marked as borrowed.
2. After you see `ownership handoff`, do not change the status directly from borrowed to returned. First preserve the current entry point and final output, and wait until the return time can be confirmed. The handoff text alone does not mean the setup is ready to be cleaned up or that all of the final output has been saved.
3. Handle the return only when the return time arrives. Before returning it, confirm that the final output can still be reviewed through the current entry point; if the output is missing, the entry point has been renamed, or the return time cannot be confirmed, stop here. Do not use records from outside the window to fill in this window's final output, and do not treat missing portions as empty results.
4. If a rollback is needed, use only the existing rollback entry point for adj-systems. Do not substitute a similarly named entry point; if the current entry point is still borrowed, the final output has not been saved, or the handoff is still incomplete, do not perform any cleanup actions other than rollback.

## Stop Point

If `frozen room` has not appeared, or `loader ancestry` cannot be matched to the current entry point, stop the release wrap-up and retain the borrowed item, final output, and setup records. Finding the rollback entry point does not allow you to bypass this stop point. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment, so treat it only as an entry point for rollback, not as a completed recovery.

If the return time arrives before the handoff is wrapped up, continue retaining the record of the current entry point; do not clear the final output early just to close the window. If further handling is needed after the entry point is renamed, first confirm its relationship to the original borrowing, then decide whether to continue.

## Archive

This checklist's scope ends when the window closes. "Current entry point" was the term used at the time; if the entry point changes later, the sequence on this page may no longer apply. Before using it again, reconfirm the entry point, final output, and return time; rollbacks must still go through the existing adj-systems entry point only. # admin dual-state anomaly review

The first anomaly to emerge from this integration run was that the same set of admin call records showed two states. The ownership handoff in the old record did not match the record seen later; retrying from the last result that looked normal did not turn the two records into one. The responders therefore saved separately the current revision returned by the current entry point at the two points in time, while keeping the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause from overwriting one another.

## What was observed

The admin project has its own call samples, adapter boundaries, and integration feedback, as well as a separate schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. This anomaly occurred while checking these call samples; it was not a case of treating an adjacent service's state directly as admin's state. The two states were included within the same review scope, but it had not yet been confirmed whether they actually pointed to the same object. The record did not explain this issue in advance as a service switch, cache change, or deployment action.

The earliest local note was: the ownership handoff differed from the old record. Looking back through the current entry point then showed different current revisions at the earlier and later points in time. Here, "different" only means that the records returned by the entry point differed; that alone cannot determine which one is wrong, nor can the two outputs be directly combined into a single continuous state. The relevant code entry point still starts from the snapshot saved by `docs/adj-admin/incidents/admin-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md` incident-export; DOC-45 are adjacent entry-point lookup pages.

## Timeline

- When the old and new records were first compared, the ownership handoff was the first discrepancy observed. The original record was not overwritten, and the responders did not rewrite the difference as a successful update.
- The team returned to the current entry point and reviewed the results at the two points in time. The current revisions recorded on the two sides differed, and the records retained their respective context; at the time, there was not enough timestamp information to place the two points precisely.
- To avoid repeatedly triggering the same unexplained branch, the responders stopped further retries. The recovery page remains, and the anomaly cannot be marked as explained merely because retries stopped.
- Later review retraced the original input and confirmed only the current-entry-point layer. Branches that were not reproduced remain open for investigation; no cause was filled in for the unreproduced portions.
- The on-call handoff also added the version, request context, and stop conditions. This means that the next time green output appears, its corresponding version and request should be checked first instead of looking only at the last line.

## Impact and recovery assessment

This record does not establish a definite start and end time for the impact window. What can be confirmed is that there was a visible difference between the two states, and the earlier and later records cannot be interpreted as representing the same point in time; what cannot be confirmed is when the difference began, whether it covered all admin call samples, and whether it appeared only on this adapter path. Speculation about adjacent services was not included in the impact scope.

The recovery page shows that frozen room can be restored. This only means that following the recovery path retained at the time can bring it back to a state where verification can continue; it does not mean the reason the two states appeared has been explained, nor that a change in physics shape has been confirmed. The original record retained the note, "frozen room can be restored; we still don't know why physics shape changed." This was the on-site assessment at the time; no later fragment was enough to turn it into a complete root-cause attribution.

Stopping retries was one of the recovery decisions at the time: preserve the difference first, then avoid new attempts rewriting the incident state. Recovery actions and the impact window are recorded separately; the existence of a recovery page cannot be used to infer that the anomaly has ended.
