# R26.9 Branch Cut Decision Record

The R26.9 branch cut review had a very narrow scope: whether Northstar Spatial Systems should move the entry window for media-frame in this branch cut. It was not a full acceptance review of interaction features, nor an attempt to consolidate all adjacent changes in the runtime into a single proposal. The materials identify only two choices: retain the current media-frame entry point, or adjust the window. The first approach maintains the current comparison baseline; the second may change the timing observed at runtime. The review did not take "possible" to mean that an improvement had already been established.

The earliest statement recorded on this page was "the window needs to be adjusted". It remains part of the historical record, but cannot be treated directly as the approved position for R26.9. That statement expressed the working assessment of the observed behavior at the time, not a decision that already provided window values, call relationships, and review results. One follow-up review did take place later, but that review did not establish facts where supporting material was missing, so the choice was narrowed to: proceed with the branch cut using the current entry point for now, with no move to the proposed window yet.

"Not moving it for now" also has a clear scope here. It does not conclude that adjusting the window will necessarily be ineffective in the future, does not conclude that the current entry point is the final location, and does not expand this review into a long-term standard for all runtime changes. The decision addresses only the entry point that can be identified at the current cut, and whether to replace it with a window that has not yet been reviewed.

## The Two Approaches Considered in the Review

| Approach | What could be confirmed at the time | What remained unresolved | Outcome for R26.9 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current media-frame entry point | The entry point remains the comparison baseline that can be repeatedly identified in the materials for this review | Questions about the current window remain | Adopted |
| Adjust the window | May change the timing observed at runtime; remains a direction for follow-up experiments | Not enough material to connect state, scenarios, and the integration tick in replay | Not adopted |

The "comparison baseline" in the table does not mean that the entry point already explains all runtime relationships. It only means that, if the entry point is not moved, subsequently observed changes can still initially be compared using the same point of reference. If the entry point and the window move at the same time, earlier observations cannot directly show where the differences come from. This distinction is the practical purpose of this choice, and the reason the adjustment proposal was not recorded as a failure.

`src/systems/bit-media-frames.js` was reviewed again. It is adjacent to the objects and call names for media-frame, so it can help locate the entry point discussed at the time. It was not treated as a permanent ownership point, nor was it written into a larger architectural relationship because of its path. The file itself serves a locating role in this decision and cannot replace the runtime comparison in replay.

## Decision Already Made

R26.9 branch cut retains the current media-frame entry, and the window will not be adjusted this round. Approval ends here. No new window value was approved, no call chain supplemented from outside the materials was approved, and no scenario that has not yet been reviewed was written into the coverage scope.

First, the entry point was retained because it leaves the cut with a stable observation target. When the entry point does not move, the subsequent ECS state, visible scene behavior, and owning integration tick are at least compared near the same entry point; when the entry point moves as well, the observation target and runtime changes change simultaneously. That difference cannot be explained solely by result screenshots or a single pass.

Second, the review requires the various observations in replay to line up with one another. The full wording in the materials is:

> Runtime changes are accepted only when ECS state, visible scene behavior, and the owning integration tick tell the same story under replay.

The role of this sentence in this decision is to limit the grounds for approval, not to require all combinations to be listed in a new table. ECS state indicates what the runtime state saw, visible scene behavior indicates what the screen or scene showed, and owning integration tick indicates what the tick responsible for that integration recorded in the same replay. If the three merely appear separately, that still cannot establish that the behavior after moving the window belongs to the same runtime change.

Again, the same-submission retries for CI cannot leave only the result. The materials explicitly require:

> same-SHA CI retries need a recorded cause

When the same SHA produces different retry results, the difference itself is not evidence for the window approach. Without a recorded cause, it is impossible to determine whether this difference is related to the entry point, the window, or the runtime state. Therefore, this round did not use the retry results to support an adjustment, nor did it add an explanation for retry causes not provided by the materials.

## Why Keep the Current Entry

The reason for keeping the current entry is not "the old one is always safe", but that this round needs to fix the comparison target first. The current material can identify the media-frame entry and use it as the basis for discussing whether the window should move; it cannot provide both a new window and a sufficient set of replay observations at the same time. If the window is moved first, then even if scene behavior changes afterward, it would still mean dealing with two changes at once: the original entry will no longer be the original entry, and the new window will also change the runtime execution sequence.

Leaving the entry in place means the questions surrounding the window do not disappear. This cost is intentional. branch cut addresses which entry this cut uses; it does not resolve all existing runtime questions. If discussion of the window continues later, the old entry will still be a reference that can be revisited; if it is moved now, the old records will need an additional distinction between the old window and the new window, and the current material has not made that distinction.

Keeping the entry also prevents two questions from being conflated. One question is "whether the current cut should switch its entry window", and the other is "whether the runtime changes in replay can be jointly explained by state, scene, and owning integration tick". The former has been decided this round; the latter has only evaluation criteria and has not been documented as completed validation. Conflating the two would make an observation that is not yet closed out look like an approved implementation adjustment.

This is also why review did not accept "the window needs adjustment" as sufficient justification. The window may indeed be something to revisit in a later comparison, but the material provides neither a specific resulting window nor replay results that separate observations before and after the adjustment. The objection to adjusting it is that the evidence is insufficient to move the comparison baseline, not a rejection of the window concept itself.

## Retaining the Unadopted Option

Adjusting the window was not included in R26.9, but it was not deleted from the record. It remains an option that was compared, because the initial draft started with exactly this question: whether the window near the existing media-frame entry should change. Removing this option would make the decision look as though it had never confronted an entry change, and would also obscure why the current entry with an open question was ultimately chosen.

The first issue with the unadopted option is that the states are not connected by the same replay. If the ECS state changes after the window changes, but visible scene behavior does not change accordingly, the window cannot be considered effective based solely on the state change; if the scene changes but there is no corresponding record of the owning integration tick, one cannot determine whether this is the expected action caused by the window; if each replay passes through a different state, even two items that happen to line up are insufficient to support the cut decision.

The second issue with the approach that was not adopted is that the retry lacks a reason. A retry of CI for the same commit can expose a difference, but the difference may come from execution conditions that have not yet been specified. The current materials do not attribute this difference to the media-frame entry point or to the window adjustment. Without a reason, the retry cannot serve as substitute evidence that "the window should be moved."

The third issue with the approach that was not adopted is that the comparison baseline will shift. Historical observations at the current entry point and new observations after the window adjustment cannot be combined without distinguishing them. If the approach is reopened later, at minimum we need to know which entry point and which window each result belongs to; otherwise, "got better" may simply mean that the comparison target changed.

These three issues are not three independent conclusions of failure. Together, they show that this round lacks the linkage needed to support an adjustment: the entry point, runtime state, visible scene, integration tick, and retry reason have not formed a single traceable record in the existing materials. Therefore, the decision is to stop at retaining the current entry point rather than continue fabricating results for the adjustment approach.

## The Turning Point in the Review

The draft presented window adjustment relatively early, making it easy for readers to see it as the primary approach and then interpret retaining the entry point as a temporary concession. That is not how the comparison actually works. The draft establishes only that the current entry point can still serve as the cut point; "the window needs to be adjusted" was merely an unreviewed working judgment. Subsequent review did not confirm what result the adjustment would produce, so this version presents the option and the decision separately.

This revision does not replace the earlier judgment with a stronger causal attribution. No material proves that the window adjustment has already failed, nor that retaining the entry point resolved the runtime issue. The revision only changes what the judgment settles on: from "the window seems to need adjustment" to "the window remains an option still to be compared, while the current cut retains the entry point." The old judgment therefore remains in its original historical context, while the current decision no longer carries forward the force of its inference.

The review also narrowed the "scope covered by the existing evidence." The scope here is not all interaction scenarios, all relevant calls, or a complete compatibility matrix. It refers only to the media-frame entry point that the current materials can identify and to how state, scene, and owning integration tick should be viewed in replay. Material beyond this scope is not automatically approved merely because it is written into the decision page.

An old simplified interpretation has also been retained: window adjustment was once treated as an action requiring only a local window change. There are no specific parameters, commands, or results corresponding to it, so it cannot be expanded further into implementation details. This trace is retained to explain why earlier records treated the window as a direct fix; the current decision does not accept this simplification, but neither does it recast it as a misattribution that the materials do not support.

## The Runtime Boundary of This Decision

Runtime changes discussed on this page must be tied back to three specific observation points, rather than assessed only by looking at a single final view. The ECS state is the observation on the state side, visible scene behavior is the observation on the scene side, and owning integration tick is the observation on the integration-execution side. The review puts them together to avoid treating improvement on any one side alone as a successful entry-window adjustment.

This does not mean that the three have already completed a successful pass in the materials. On the contrary, the review criteria spell out the mutual corroboration required to accept runtime changes, while the current decision provides no new set of results of that kind. That is the basis for the judgment to stop here this time, not a supplement to replay output that was not provided.

If only ECS state is retained, readers can tell that something changed on the state side, but not whether the visible scene followed; if only visible scene behavior is retained, the display may look normal, but there is no way to show that the state updated in the same order; if only owning integration tick is retained, a single tick's record cannot by itself prove that the scene behavior in the replay was stable. Only by putting all three back into the same replay is there a chance to determine whether the window change is worth pursuing through another cut.

The "same replay" here is not a generalized testing slogan either. It addresses the question of when to compare. Different replays, different entry points, or CI retries for which no reason is given cannot be directly treated as the same runtime story. The current materials do not provide additional replay IDs, output snippets, or window parameters, so this page does not fill in those details.

The decision at the time can be understood through the following relationship:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[R26.9 branch cut] --> B[Retain the current media-frame entry]
    A --> C[Adjust the window]
    B --> D[Use the current entry as the comparison baseline]
    C --> E[A common observation is needed in the replay]
    E --> F[ECS state]
    E --> G[visible scene behavior]
    E --> H[owning integration tick]
    F --> I[same-SHA CI retries need a recorded cause]
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J[The existing materials are insufficient to approve adjusting the window]
```

The two branches in the diagram are the two approaches actually compared during review. The right side is not a process that was already executed and failed; rather, it is the observation relationship that the adjustment proposal must address. The endpoint states the result of this round: the current materials are insufficient to bring the window adjustment into the branch cut, so the decision was to return to the current entry on the left.

## Compatibility cost

Keeping the current entry point has a clear cost of deferral. Questions about the window will remain, and subsequent runtime observations may continue to be debated. The branch cut will not automatically answer whether the window is appropriate simply because the entry point is retained. If later records only note that "the entry point was not changed," but forget that the window issue remains unresolved, the old questions will lose their context in the new records.

The compatibility cost of adjusting the window, on the other hand, is shifting the comparison baseline. Existing records were built around the current entry point; if new records are built around a different window, they cannot simply be stitched together in chronological order. Readers need to know which window each observation belongs to before they can determine whether a result reflects a change in behavior or a change in what is being compared. The current material does not make this distinction, so this decision does not take on the explanatory burden of shifting the baseline.

The compatibility cost discussed here is limited to the subject under review. No material identifies a specific external caller, a specific version difference, or a specific scenario, so this cannot be expanded into an account of the impact on all consumers. Nor does any material show a failure that has been attributed to the current entry point, so retaining the entry point cannot be described as an incident fix.

Likewise, adjusting the window has not been ruled out permanently. If subsequent material only shows a single visual change, or only a single CI retry result, that will still not be enough to change this decision. The material needs to distinguish between the entry point and the window, and correlate ECS state, visible scene behavior, and owning integration tick with one another in replay; retries of the same commit also need an explanation. This condition describes the material missing for a renewed comparison, not a checklist of work items already completed.

## Objections

The objection to keeping the entry point is straightforward: if the window itself is the source of the observed behavior, continuing to use the current window may merely push the problem past the branch cut. This objection has not been rejected. The decision only holds that, without material that can explain the outcome of the adjustment, moving the window would change both the frame of reference and the runtime observations, so it cannot be treated as a safe choice for this round's cut.

Another objection concerns CI retries. If the same SHA produces different outputs, continuing to use the current entry point cannot explain the difference either. This objection is also valid, but it does not imply that "the window should therefore be adjusted." The lack of an explanation only means that retry results cannot serve as a basis for the choice for now; it does not justify assigning them a cause, much less establishing an unverified causal relationship between them and a window adjustment.

Another easy misreading is: since the review requires the three types of observations to tell the same story in replay, the adjustment should be approved as long as all three ultimately appear consistent. This reading is still too broad. The review material does not provide a new window, a specific replay, or completed results; the requirement describes how to make the judgment, which does not mean that the material already meets that standard. The decision keeps the current entry point precisely because this step has not yet happened.

These reservations have not been developed into a separate alternative proposal. They center on the costs and gaps of the same choice: the current entry point preserves the reference but leaves questions about the window; adjusting the window may change timing, but lacks a shared replay and records of the reasons. Splitting them into multiple items that were never provided would make a one-page, narrowly scoped decision appear to cover more ground than the material actually supports.

## Past Examples in the Record

The following two old statements remain in the historical record, but do not serve as current decisions:

- "The window needs adjustment": an early working assessment, indicating that the entry window was considered a possible direction for improvement at the time; there was no corresponding specific window or review result.
- "The retry results differ, so the window is worth moving": an inference method that later ceased to apply. Different results first indicate that a difference occurred, but cannot on their own show that moving the window is justified.

These statements are retained not to let old assessments continue to guide the branch cut, but to preserve the disagreements that existed as the decision took shape. If only the final statement, "retain the current entry point", were left, later readers would not see why the other path was not adopted or what exactly the review narrowed down. Wording from the old examples may be cited to explain historical shifts, but must not be treated as new facts.

The old examples also reveal two distinct errors. The first treats a possible local adjustment as an already sufficient solution; the second treats a difference in results as a reason for adjustment. Both skip over the connection between the entry point, the window, and replay observations. The current decision has not filled in these two logical leaps to reach an implementation conclusion, but simply no longer relies on them when making the choice.

## What is retained, and what is deferred

Only one decision has been retained: the R26.9 branch cut retains the current media-frame entry point, and window adjustments are not included in this cut. This decision can be reviewed because the comparison targets are clear, and adoption and non-adoption are recorded separately.

What is deferred is whether the window will be worth moving later. Deferral is neither approval nor an attribution of failure. New material is still needed to explain at which entry point and window the change occurred, and whether the three categories of observations in replay belong to the same runtime process. The existing content does not provide this material, so no specific operational steps are specified for it in advance.

Also deferred is the explanation for retries of the same SHA. The page retains the requirement same-SHA CI retries need a recorded cause, but does not specify a cause. Identifying the cause as a particular environment, execution path, or other factor would go beyond what the current record can support; at present, only the need to record a cause can be confirmed, not what that cause is.

The reviewed file path is also retained only as a locator. It helps indicate which local object was examined at the time, but does not change the decision about the current entry point, establish that the file is the long-term owner, or provide caller relationships beyond the material. Elevating the path directly into an ownership conclusion would misread the location of a review as a design decision.

## Gaps to address first when reopening the window

If window adjustments are compared again in the future, the first step is not to rewrite "The window needs adjustment" as a decision, but to label the old entry point and the new window separately first. Only then can the old records and new observations avoid overwriting one another on the same timeline. The current material does not provide a name or value for the new window, and this page does not assign it a name.

The second step requires putting the observations from the replay into the same record. When ECS state, visible scene behavior, owning integration tick appear separately, they can only indicate isolated phenomena. Only when they correspond to one another within the same replay might they support a decision to accept the runtime changes. Here, "might" still does not mean approval, because the decision must still be based on the actual evidence.

The third step requires recording the reasons for same-SHA CI retries. Differences in results can remain phenomena that need to be explained, but they must not be attributed to the window upfront. If the record of reasons does not identify the corresponding entry point and window, it is still insufficient to change the comparison baseline; this page does not add execution context that has not been provided.

These three gaps need to be considered together because filling only one of them would still leave ambiguity. Adding only the window name does not explain the runtime results; adding only replay visuals does not explain whether ECS state and tick belong to the same process; adding only the reasons for CI retries does not explain whether the adjusted window is effective either. They are not a new checklist of approval conditions, but the specific gaps that explain why this round's decision stays with the current entry point.

## Final Wording for the Record

This branch cut will proceed with the current media-frame entry point. Adjusting the window was an option that was reviewed but not adopted, because the available materials are insufficient to align ECS state, visible scene behavior and owning integration tick in the replay, and no usable record of the reasons for same-SHA CI retries was left.

This statement does not elevate the current entry point to the final architecture, does not deem adjusting the window permanently wrong, and does not present a single file review as proof of a call relationship. It only records what was chosen at the R26.9 cut, and why the comparison baseline was not moved within that same cut. If new materials become available later, first identify the entry point and window to which the observations correspond, then assess whether those materials truly change this decision; until then, the previous proposal and reservations remain on the page.

# WebXR Device Matrix Transition Handoff

For this transition, we won't initially treat the device matrix as a device list that has to be replaced all at once. The handoff covers the process of moving known media-controls consumers from the old entry point to the candidate path; each handoff must clearly identify a specific entity state, the room conditions at the time, and a trace that can reproduce that state.

First, list the confirmed consumers and the old entry points they still use. Include only known callers in the list; do not count assumed consumers toward migration completion. Then select one of those consumers that can roll back on its own to try the candidate path. This consumer must be able to return to its original entry point; do not run the first trial at a call site that cannot be restored.

At handoff, provide three things along with the consumer: the entity's state, the conditions in the room, and where to start looking in the trace. The recipient does not need to take on the entire matrix up front; confirming one boundary is enough, such as whether that entity state can still be reproduced through the candidate path under those room conditions. Do not expand to other consumers until that boundary has been confirmed.

Recovery is also per consumer: roll back this one trial call, return to its original old entry point, and keep the traces from before and after the rollback. This lets us distinguish issues in the candidate path itself from differences caused by room conditions.

If the caller population has not been fully counted, or the trial consumer cannot roll back on its own, this page remains marked as migration in progress.

# WebXR Device Matrix Cutover Handoff

The device matrix cutover is still being rolled out per consumer, rather than putting all WebXR devices into one batch. The old entry point for media-controls is the starting point for this migration; the candidate path is first validated with a single consumer that can roll back independently. Whether subsequent consumers join depends on the receiving party confirming one clearly defined boundary, not on whether the device name already appears in the inventory.

```text
Before cutover: known consumers → media-controls old entry point
                         ↑ Can be rolled back by consumer

After trial: one consumer that can roll back independently → candidate path → boundary confirmation
Remaining known consumers ────────→ old entry point
```

## Lock down the old boundary before migration

Inventory starts with the known consumers of media-controls. For each consumer, record at least the old entry point, current entity state, applicable room conditions, and a reproducible trace. Here, "known" only means the caller population counted so far; if there is no evidence that something is in use, do not write it down as a migration target just to complete the matrix.

Entity state must be recorded as a concrete state recognizable to the receiving party, not a blanket judgment such as "interaction is normal." Room conditions should be included with the record as well, because behavior observed after the same consumer leaves its original conditions cannot be attributed directly to the candidate path. The trace is the handoff's reference point: the receiving party needs to use it to reproduce this state, rather than guess what happened earlier from the device or room name.

When locating the old entry point, you can start with `src/hub.js` and the call name used at the time. This is only the anchor for this round of tracing; it does not mean that this file has permanently assumed ownership of the device matrix. If a consumer cannot be confirmed further from here, leave it on the old entry point and place it in a later batch once the caller inventory is complete.

## Let only one consumer take the candidate path first

The first-round consumer has one hard requirement: it must be able to roll back independently. Specifically, self-rollback means that the consumer Fang Ke can abandon the candidate path and restore its original old entry point, without moving any other known consumers at the same time or first changing the entire room setup to a different configuration.

Before the trial, lock this consumer's entity state and room conditions in place, then capture a trace. After that, change only this consumer's path selection. Do not expand the caller set at the same time or bring different room conditions into the same trial; even if the behavior changes, there would be no way to determine whether the change came from the path or the conditions.

The first-round result is not "the candidate path is generally usable." The receiving party confirms only one boundary: whether this consumer can obtain a reproducible result along the candidate path with this entity state and these room conditions. Only after that confirmation is complete may you select the next known consumer and repeat the same handoff. Until the first boundary is confirmed, the rest of the matrix remains on the old entry point.

## Minimum contents of the handoff package

Records handed to the receiving party are organized around one trial, not abstract device categories:

- The consumer name and the media-controls old entry point it originally used;
- The concrete entity state during the trial;
- The room conditions to maintain;
- Traces from before and after the trial that can be used for reproduction;
- The action that restores this consumer to the old entry point;
- The one boundary the receiving party needs to confirm.

The reason for this format is that the receiving party takes on only one local judgment. If the only thing on hand is the conclusion "migrated to the candidate path," with no state, conditions, or trace, a later difference cannot be used to determine whether to return to the old entry point or first reproduce the original trial. Conversely, the handoff package does not declare on the receiving party's behalf that the other consumers have completed migration.

For the receiving party, the confirmation order is fixed: first reproduce this entity state from the trace, then check the room conditions, and finally assess only the candidate path's behavior within this boundary. If any step cannot be reproduced, stop with this consumer and do not propagate the unconfirmed state to the next batch. This stopping point is part of the migration cadence, not a way to leave the problem for a later entry point without context.

## Restore the old path

Rollback restores only the trial consumer. Keep the trace from the candidate path first, then point this consumer back to its original media-controls old entry point; after restoration, capture another trace with the same entity state and room conditions. The two records should show which path was used before and after the trial.

Do not roll back other consumers at the same time just because "the candidate path looks unsuitable." The other callers did not participate in the trial; simply leave them on the old entry point. If the restoration action itself depends on another consumer, another room condition, or a trace that cannot be obtained, this consumer does not meet the first-round requirement and should be removed from the candidate batch.

The initial draft described rollback as a remedial action after cutover. After review, it was changed into a first-round selection criterion: first confirm that the consumer can be restored, then allow it to take the candidate path. This change avoids mistaking an unrollbackable call site for a validation sample and gives the receiving party a repeatable local handoff instead of a vague migration commitment.

## What remains in the migration

While the caller population has not been fully counted, do not infer from the first-round result that the entire device matrix has been migrated. Even after the first-round boundary is confirmed, that only shows that this combination of entity state, room conditions, and consumer can continue to be handled. Start the next batch's records again from the known consumers and the old entry point.

For tracking related to the incident review entry point for media-frame, see DOC-53; this page retains only the consumers, candidate path, and rollback handoff for the device matrix cutover.
